findings.topic: SPV vs full nodes: one essay reverses the corpus's core doctrine

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: SPV is second-class epistemically — full nodes know, SPV clients merely believe — and users are advised to run a full node as the architecture of sovereignty.

sources.title: Private Keys, Proofs, and the Illusion of Ownership in Digital Cash Systems
sources.quote: SPV clients believe; full nodes know.

sources.title: Private Keys, Proofs, and the Illusion of Ownership in Digital Cash Systems
sources.quote: Education is "the architecture of sovereignty": understand key architecture, master hardware wallets, verify Merkle branches manually, run a full node.

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: SPV is the whitepaper's designed and provably sufficient mode for all non-mining users; non-mining full nodes are causally inert spectators who contribute nothing to security or governance.

sources.title: A Mechanism of Honour - Ledger of Blood and Electricity
sources.quote: SPV is "not merely a shortcut—it is the only road worth walking"; full-node operators are "parasites. They are barnacles on the hull".

sources.title: The Cult of the Full Node
sources.quote: SPV is not a compromise. It is the civilised form of verification for a system that intends to grow up and take responsibility for humanity's scale.

sources.title: Verification Without Enforcement Is Observation, Not Security
sources.quote: Craig's peer-reviewed paper (accepted at IEEE CCNCPS 2026) proves formally that SPV is the Nash equilibrium for all non-mining participants... a non-mining node running incompatible rules has exactly the causal influence of one that is switched off.

findings.analysis: Position A claims full nodes confer knowledge and sovereignty that SPV cannot; Position B claims non-mining full nodes have identically zero causal effect and that SPV is the rational, designed equilibrium. These cannot both be true, and the outlier (2025-10-15) sits chronologically between essays of the opposing campaign (2025-07-30, 2025-12-15, 2026-03-24), so it is not an evolution of view. The collision is at the user-security level, not just the network level: verification-without-enforcement explicitly asks whether running a full node makes you more secure and answers no.
findings.resolution: null

findings.topic: Immutability as 'only defence' vs court-ordered freezing/reassignment (DAR)

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: Bitcoin's survival depends on absolute immutability; freezing spendable coins by decree is expropriation, and Ethereum's DAO fork 'violated its own immutability in the name of investor relief'.

sources.title: Set in Stone or Sold to the Highest Bidder: Why Immutability Is Bitcoin's Only Defence
sources.quote: The system either is set in stone, or it is rewritten by the hands with the fattest wallets and the greasiest fingers.

sources.title: The Theft That Never Was
sources.quote: Freezing dormant coins renders currently spendable outputs unspendable "not by the actions of their holders, but by the decree of those modifying the protocol. This is not preservation. It is expropriation."

sources.title: The Necessity of the Stone: Protocol Finality, Political Intrusion, and the Integrity of Bitcoin
sources.quote: Fixing the fundamental rules — transaction formats, signature validation, block structure, proof of work, and the issuance schedule — removes politics from money's foundation... no council, no emergency provision, no negotiation.

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: On BSV, courts can order UTXOs frozen and reassigned: a notary broadcasts the order via the Blacklist Manager and miners activate the freeze; compliance is a mandatory legal obligation, and recovering keyless coins is lawful reintroduction, not theft.

sources.title: Transparency Is Not Centralisation: NAR, DAR, and the Legal Architecture of Blockchain Governance
sources.quote: DAR operates in four steps: plaintiff litigates ownership; obtains a freeze order or injunction; a designated notary translates the order into machine-readable form broadcast via the Blacklist Manager; miners activate the freeze upon consensus among honest nodes.

sources.title: The Miner Is Not a Monarch
sources.quote: Compliance with valid court orders over identifiable property is mandatory legal obligation, not discretionary governance... refusal "does not create freedom. It creates liability."

sources.title: The Theft That Never Was
sources.quote: One does not commit theft by recovering abandoned property. One reintroduces it into use.

findings.analysis: The same technical act — miners making a validly signed UTXO unspendable — is 'expropriation' when done by protocol modification (BTC quantum-freeze proposals, Ethereum's DAO fork) and 'judicially mediated enforcement of property rights' when done by BSV's DAR. A ledger whose state courts can reverse sits awkwardly with 'What's immutable can't be owned. What's fixed can't be bought', and with signature validation being listed among the rules set in stone. What hangs on it: whether 'immutability' was ever a claim about the ledger state, or only ever about the rule set.
findings.resolution: Craig supplies a three-category distinction (transparency-is-not-centralisation): (1) altering consensus rules, (2) altering transaction-validity conditions, (3) enforcement action within an unchanged protocol — DAR is claimed to operate exclusively in category (3), triggered by courts with due process, so protocol immutability is preserved while the ledger state remains answerable to law. The residual strain he does not address: a frozen UTXO cannot be spent despite a mathematically valid signature, which his critics would place in category (2).

findings.topic: 'No spam in a priced system' vs DAR/NAR admission control

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: Permissionlessness means admission conditioned only on objective validity and payment; any system that sorts among paying users by payload, purpose or 'standardness' has instituted a permission regime — even dispersed, polycentric filtering is a regulatory regime.

sources.title: There Is No Such Thing as Spam in a Priced System
sources.quote: Any system that sorts among paying users by payload, purpose, "standardness" or escalating penalties has instituted a permission regime, acquired regulators, and abandoned the permissionlessness that made it distinctive.

sources.title: There Is No Such Thing as Spam in a Priced System
sources.quote: "permissionless" means admission conditioned only on objective validity and payment... Everything in Gate 2 is governance, whatever the software calls it.

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: BSV operates a Gate-2 filter by design: the Blacklist Manager broadcasts court-ordered freezes that miners enforce, and transactions linked to criminality can be isolated, quarantined and removed.

sources.title: Transparency Is Not Centralisation: NAR, DAR, and the Legal Architecture of Blockchain Governance
sources.quote: A designated notary translates the order into machine-readable form broadcast via the Blacklist Manager; miners activate the freeze upon consensus among honest nodes.

sources.title: A Mechanism of Honour - Ledger of Blood and Electricity
sources.quote: Transactions linked to criminality "can be isolated, quarantined, and removed".

findings.analysis: A spend of a frozen UTXO is consensus-valid (Gate 1) and fee-paying, yet is rejected on the basis of the legal status of the funds — sorting by 'purpose', which the spam essay's own framework (Yeung's standard-setting/information-gathering/enforcement test) classifies as algorithmic regulation and a permission regime. Under the definitions of the August 2026 essay, BSV-with-DAR is a permissioned network; under the DAR essays, that same filtering is the normalisation of Bitcoin. Both cannot hold under one definition of permissionless.
findings.resolution: Attempted via layer separation in the-miner-is-not-a-monarch ("Code is procedure. Law concerns rights.") — legal validity sits above protocol validity, so DAR is law, not policy. But the spam essay explicitly denies that dispersal or motive changes the classification (Black 2008: a dispersed filter "remains a polycentric regulatory regime"), so the reconciliation is asserted, not derived.

findings.topic: Censorship-resistance definition vs the Blacklist Manager

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: Censorship resistance is the structural property that no non-miner can prevent the inclusion of a fee-paying transaction; filtering coalitions are structurally impotent because fresh addresses give no shared object to filter.

sources.title: The Two Tiers Are a Market, Not a Cage
sources.quote: Censorship resistance is the structural property that no non-miner can prevent the inclusion of a fee-paying transaction.

sources.title: Censorship Resistance, Atomic Settlement, and the Limits of Coalition Power
sources.quote: Unlike the OFAC SDN list, fresh addresses provide no shared object to filter... The coalition would need to coordinate not on a list of identified objects but on a classifier.

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: Eight days later, court orders routed through a non-miner notary (the Blacklist Manager) oblige miners to block specific UTXOs — a shared list, coordinated enforcement, and liability for refusal.

sources.title: The Miner Is Not a Monarch
sources.quote: If a court determines a UTXO belongs to Party A, the miner's role is operational compliance; refusal "does not create freedom. It creates liability."

sources.title: Transparency Is Not Centralisation: NAR, DAR, and the Legal Architecture of Blockchain Governance
sources.quote: A designated notary translates the order into machine-readable form broadcast via the Blacklist Manager; miners activate the freeze upon consensus among honest nodes.

findings.analysis: The definition as stated contains no lawfulness carve-out, and DAR is precisely a non-miner mechanism preventing inclusion of fee-paying transactions, coordinated on a broadcast list — the structure the censorship essays say cannot exist. There is also a pincer with his own privacy work: if fresh single-use keys defeat list-based filtering (censorship-resistance-atomic-settlement, and the drizzle-wallet essays), then DAR's blacklist only bites against static, identifiable UTXOs — meaning either the privacy techniques undermine lawful recovery or lawful recovery undermines the privacy claims.
findings.resolution: An implicit carve-out exists across the DAR essays: censorship resistance protects lawful transactions, while a frozen UTXO is adjudicated the property of another, so blocking it is not censorship but enforcement. That carve-out is never written into the censorship-resistance definition itself.

findings.topic: 'No governance, no administrators' vs BSV's stewardship apparatus

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: The design ideal is a system with no administrators and no governance at all — rules not open to negotiation because no one holds the pen.

sources.title: The Necessity of the Stone: Protocol Finality, Political Intrusion, and the Integrity of Bitcoin
sources.quote: These elements are the constitution of Bitcoin, not the policies of its administrators. They are not open to negotiation because the system has no administrators.

sources.title: Set in Stone
sources.quote: Design one: base set forever — Script fully enabled, block capacity unbounded by protocol, no upgrade mechanism, no governance, because "the rules are not in question"... The absence of governance is not a deficiency to be remedied — it is the entire point.

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: BSV in fact has a named steward: the BSV Association defends the lock, publishes the Network Access Rules as a contract, operates a restored alert system, and designates the DAR notary.

sources.title: Who Controls the Rules? Governance Credibility and the $109 Billion Question
sources.quote: The BSV lock (post-Genesis 2020; script, UTXO structure and incentives frozen, defended by the BSV Association; Ĝ = 0.85–1.00).

sources.title: Transparency Is Not Centralisation: NAR, DAR, and the Legal Architecture of Blockchain Governance
sources.quote: The NAR is a published unilateral contract: offer to an indefinite class, acceptance by performance... The NAR is also bilateral, constraining the steward as much as participants.

sources.title: Authority Without Command: The Alert Key, Coordination, and the System That Might Have Been
sources.quote: The BSV Association's Alert System is explicitly a restoration of the Satoshi-era alert key that BTC Core discarded.

findings.analysis: The absolutist 'no governance' rhetoric coexists with an operational governance apparatus (steward, published access rules, alert key, blacklist notary). His own credibility metric rescues the substance — a controller who locks the rules scores highly — but then the differentiator is lock-credibility, not absence of governance, and the rhetoric overshoots the measurement. What hangs on it: whether 'decentralisation' claims for BSV are made on the governance axis he tells others to measure.
findings.resolution: who-controls-the-rules-governance: "Governance credibility depends on what the controller does, not on whether a controller exists"; transparency-is-not-centralisation: published rules plus an external judicial trigger are "transparency, not centralisation".

findings.topic: The decentralisation vector is measured on BTC/ETH but never on BSV

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: Decentralisation is a vector (admission, consensus, governance, mutability) summarised by its minimum layer; reporting one flattering metric is selection bias, and legal-jurisdiction and sponsor concentration must be included.

sources.title: Effective Decentralisation Is the Minimum, Not the Average
sources.quote: A system cannot be more decentralised than its most concentrated effective control layer... Reporting one flattering metric (usually validator or hash distribution) as "decentralisation" is selection bias, not measurement.

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: The actual measurements are computed for Bitcoin and Ethereum; BSV appears only as future work, and is defended instead by legal reclassification, with the chokepoint conceded.

sources.title: Who Actually Controls a Blockchain? An Economist's Map of the Power Structure
sources.quote: Separability is measured with a Jaccard index over actor sets... computed for Ethereum and Bitcoin over 2022Q4–2025Q3... The hazard-model extension explicitly names Bitcoin Cash, Bitcoin SV, and Ethereum Classic as the fork panel for future work.

sources.title: Concentration Is Not Centralisation
sources.quote: Industrial concentration — five to twenty serious miners — is the normal oligopolistic equilibrium of a capital-intensive Proof-of-Work security industry.

sources.title: Transparency Is Not Centralisation: NAR, DAR, and the Legal Architecture of Blockchain Governance
sources.quote: He argues like a lawyer rather than a partisan — conceding the points that have force (the chokepoint exists; Howey is fact-sensitive) and then distinguishing them.

findings.analysis: Under Deff = min(layers), BSV's score would be bound by its most concentrated layers — a single-Association governance layer and a miner set at or below the low end of his own five-to-twenty 'normal' band — yet the instrument is never run on BSV. The asymmetry matters because the entire measurement programme is framed as replacing slogans with numbers; for his own chain the numbers are replaced by legal argument.
findings.resolution: Partial: effective-decentralisation-is-the notes that "concentrated governance over a low-mutability rule set is constrained governance", and concentration-is-not-centralisation separates market structure from rule-setting power — together implying BSV's concentrated layers are harmless because mutability is locked. That is a qualitative exemption, not a measurement.

findings.topic: Alert key under a Bitcoin Foundation vs foundation-led governance scoring near zero

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: The Satoshi-era alert key should have been preserved under structured stewardship — explicitly, a functional Bitcoin Foundation under Gavin Andresen — letting miners coordinate, including rejecting transaction classes, on an authenticated signal.

sources.title: Authority Without Command: The Alert Key, Coordination, and the System That Might Have Been
sources.quote: Had it been preserved under structured stewardship — such as a functional Bitcoin Foundation under Gavin Andresen — it could have supported a rational, miner-led and merchant-aware response layer for system integrity.

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: Three weeks earlier, foundation-led governance systems were measured at near-zero rule credibility.

sources.title: Who Controls the Rules? Governance Credibility and the $109 Billion Question
sources.quote: Developer-led, foundation-led and token-voting systems cluster near zero; only explicit protocol locks exceed 0.60... The only way to get above 0.60 is to stop changing the rules.

findings.analysis: The essay mourns the loss of an identifiable, foundation-stewarded coordination key immediately after his own dataset scored foundation-led stewardship at Ĝ ≈ 0.10. The wobble is softened because the alert key signals rather than changes rules — but its flagship use case (coordinated rejection of transaction classes) is admission control, which his spam essay classifies as governance.
findings.resolution: The alert 'informed without compelling' — signalling is not rule-change — and elsewhere in the corpus identifiable authority is affirmatively a security feature (why-hash-power-is-not-security: "identifiable authority is itself a security feature").

findings.topic: Quantum 'fraud' vs engineered post-quantum defences

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: Quantum computing is a sustained, structural funding fraud; no logical qubit has ever been built and none is coming on any physics-supported timeline.

sources.title: Quantum Computing Is a Multi-Hundred-Billion-Dollar Fraud
sources.quote: No logical qubit has ever been built... The product does not exist. The people selling it know the product does not exist. The fraud is not accidental.

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: He nonetheless publishes exact-byte post-quantum constructions for Bitcoin — hash-committed nonces, a 10,423-byte WOTS+ verifier, fragmentation wallets — and a post-quantum digital-cash system design.

sources.title: Quantum-Ineffective Bitcoin: A Script-Level, Hash-Anchored Defence Against Hypothetical Quantum Key Recovery
sources.quote: Even granting a fault-tolerant quantum computer that can recover ECDSA private keys from exposed public keys (Shor-level capability), Bitcoin remains secure as digital cash without any protocol change.

sources.title: The Quantum Apocalypse Is Coming Any Decade Now, So Here Is the Solution to a Problem That Will Not Exist
sources.quote: Not believer's enthusiasm. Insurance.

sources.title: Post-Quantum Digital Cash
sources.quote: He opens by noting he believes QC is "a scam" that will not arrive in his grandchildren's lives, but models the case as promoted.

findings.analysis: Belt-and-braces or contradiction? On its face he is selling engineering against a machine he calls a press-release fiction. The corpus is unusually explicit that this is expected-value insurance (<1% in ten years) plus compliance capture (NIST/ETSI/EBA demand it), so the tension is rhetorical rather than logical — though the insurance framing sits oddly beside the fraud framing, since one does not usually buy insurance against a non-existent peril unless regulators force the purchase, which is his actual position.
findings.resolution: Explicit and repeated: his probability estimates (under 1% in ten years), the cheapness of native-Script defences requiring no protocol change, and the compliance regime's demand — "three percent of catastrophic loss is enough to motivate cheap precautions" (the-quantum-apocalypse-is-coming).

findings.topic: Payment channels as rent-extraction (April) vs payment channels as engineering (May)

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: Off-chain mechanisms — payment channels, federated sidechains, bridges, rollups — are by economic function third-party rent-extractors; a scaled base layer needs none of them.

sources.title: The Toll Road You Were Promised Would Be Free: How Refusing to Scale Rebuilds the Banks
sources.quote: A base layer that cannot carry demanded transaction volume pushes activity into off-chain systems that are, by economic function, third-party rent-extractors — payment channels, federated sidechains, bridges, rollups... a scaled base layer needs no channels, federations, bridges, or rollups at all.

sources.title: Lightning's Velvet Manacles: Watchtowers, Custody, and the Quiet Return of Shadow Banking
sources.quote: Lightning's security model punishes inattention with confiscation and therefore demands perpetual vigilance... so they rationally outsource each burden to watchtowers, hubs and custodial wallets.

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: Hash chains, payment channels and blind e-cash are original-protocol mechanisms that decouple payments from settlements; he designs sellable hash-chain micropayments via channels plus e-cash tokens, and celebrates an EVM Layer 2 (BSVM) on BSV with a bridge covenant.

sources.title: The Immutable Stock and the Unbounded Flow
sources.quote: Hash chains, payment channels, and blind e-cash decouple the count of payments from the count of on-chain settlements... A channel that processes a million updates writes twice to the chain — once to open, once to close.

sources.title: Selling the Unspent Chain
sources.quote: Residual trust is reduced to a platform trusted only for liveness and correct execution.

sources.title: What Siggi Built
sources.quote: BSVM is an EVM L2 on BSV in which every state transition is authorised by a STARK validity proof verified on-chain inside a Rúnar-compiled Script covenant, with no sequencer.

findings.analysis: The generic term 'payment channels' is condemned categorically in April and engineered approvingly in May; the toll-road essay's list does not distinguish bilateral channels from routed hub networks, and BSVM is literally a bridge-plus-L2 of the kind the same essay calls 'a trust downgrade dressed as a feature upgrade'. The corpus's own distinctions (bilateral vs routed; complement to a scaled base vs substitute for a throttled one; on-chain settlement vs hub custody) do real work but are not made in the polemic.
findings.resolution: the-immutable-stock-and-the-unbounded: "off-chain constructions complement an immutable base rather than fix a broken one" — channels were in the 2009 protocol (nSequence), so using them is 'use, not revision'; the Lightning critique targets the penalty/watchtower/routing model built to compensate for a throttled base, not bilateral channels on a scaled chain.

findings.topic: 'The script is the law' vs 'code is law was never true'

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: Within the identity architecture, script enforcement replaces administrative and legal grace entirely.

sources.title: Native On-Chain Identity: capability-first, passwordless, and self-recovering
sources.quote: Recovery is not administrative grace; it is cryptographic certainty... The script is the law.

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: 'Code is law' is philosophically primitive and was never true: code settles the ledger, law settles the rights.

sources.title: The Law of Controlled Amnesia
sources.quote: Code may settle the ledger. Law settles the rights.

sources.title: The Miner Is Not a Monarch
sources.quote: The claim "code is law" was "always philosophically primitive".

findings.analysis: A slogan-level collision between the corpus's own maximalist and anti-maximalist poles. The identity essay's pitch is precisely that cryptographic self-recovery makes legal/administrative recourse unnecessary — the absolutism the law essays dismantle, and one that DAR overrides in practice (a court can reassign what script enforced). Reconcilable by domain (in-protocol enforcement vs legal entitlement), but the slogans as printed are flatly opposed.
findings.resolution: Implicit domain separation: script governs capability inside the protocol; law governs rights outside it. Never stated alongside the identity essay's slogan.

findings.topic: On-chain identity vs 'the blockchain records transactions, not identity'

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: Identity should be rebuilt as a capability proven inside the transaction; a valid signature or script evaluation is the only identity that matters.

sources.title: Native On-Chain Identity: capability-first, passwordless, and self-recovering
sources.quote: A valid signature or script evaluation inside a transaction is the only identity that matters.

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: The chain cannot attest identity at all: a signature proves control of a key and nothing more, and legal enforceability requires attribution to an identifiable person.

sources.title: The Gospel According to Grok
sources.quote: The blockchain records transactions, not identity; a signature proves control of a key and nothing more.

sources.title: The Mark That Belongs to No One
sources.quote: A signature satisfies the signature requirement for enforcement only if it is attributable to an identifiable legal person.

findings.analysis: The word 'identity' carries two senses — cryptographic capability (what a key can do) versus legal attribution (who the key belongs to) — and the corpus's identity architecture and its Satoshi-keys critique lean on opposite senses. The tension is real at the rhetoric level ('the only identity that matters' vs 'not identity'), even though the underlying positions are compatible.
findings.resolution: The capability/attribution distinction, bridged by digital-identity-and-the-architecture (2025-10-28): self-managed key-held credentials with the state attesting facts at issuance — capability on-chain, personhood attested off-chain.

findings.topic: 'Set in stone since 2009' vs BSV's own Genesis rule-change in 2020

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: The original 2009 design was complete and should never have been touched; protocol identity is fidelity to the rule — the original is the chain that kept the rule.

sources.title: Set in Stone or Sold to the Highest Bidder: Why Immutability Is Bitcoin's Only Defence
sources.quote: Bitcoin "should be boring. It should be blunt. It should be exactly the same tomorrow as it was in 2009."

sources.title: IPv4.1 Does Not Exist
sources.quote: The original is the chain that kept the rule.

sources.title: Set in Stone
sources.quote: Design one: base set forever — Script fully enabled, block capacity unbounded by protocol, no upgrade mechanism, no governance, because "the rules are not in question".

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: BSV's current rule set was itself installed by a rule-changing event — the Genesis upgrade of February 2020 — and the 'lock' only begins after it.

sources.title: The Quantum Apocalypse Is Coming Any Decade Now, So Here Is the Solution to a Problem That Will Not Exist
sources.quote: The enabler is BSV's Genesis upgrade (February 2020), which restored OP_CAT and the rest of Satoshi's opcode set.

sources.title: What Siggi Built
sources.quote: Only the Genesis restoration (February 2020) of Satoshi's opcodes and removal of size caps makes an 85 KB on-chain FRI verifier possible.

sources.title: Who Controls the Rules? Governance Credibility and the $109 Billion Question
sources.quote: The BSV lock (post-Genesis 2020; script, UTXO structure and incentives frozen, defended by the BSV Association; Ĝ = 0.85–1.00).

findings.analysis: If the 2009 design was complete and untouchable, needing a 2020 'restoration' concedes the chain's rules were changed twice — the BTC-era disabling and the BSV-era re-enabling — and that a coalition with effective rule-changing power existed as late as 2020. His own fidelity criterion ('the chain that kept the rule') rewards continuity, which restoration is not; and his G metric scores BSV's lock only from 2020. The tension is between the immutability rhetoric's timeless frame and the corpus's own dated history of the chain he champions.
findings.resolution: The restoration framing: Genesis undoes deviations and returns to the 2009 rule set, so the lock starts once the original is reinstated. geography-of-discretion adds that reserved extension points are 'use, not revision' — though OP_CAT was disabled, not reserved, so re-enabling it is a rule change even on his own taxonomy.

findings.topic: Law inside the security model vs the mapped limits of law

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: Legal deterrence already backstops Bitcoin's security for every economically significant transaction, because industrial miners are identifiable and jurisdictionally reachable.

sources.title: The Law Already Inside Bitcoin
sources.quote: Bitcoin's security does not depend on being beyond the law. It depends on being embedded in it... Legal irrelevance does not scale with transaction value. It scales against it.

sources.title: The Lawless Blockchain Is a Story We Tell for Small Change
sources.quote: Over 98% of hash power is attributable to publicly identifiable operators. The value at which the legal term first turns positive is estimated at roughly $1m–$4.25m.

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: Four days earlier he mapped a ~50% hole in that reach: US and Chinese legal machinery cannot touch each other's pools, and the China-linked side is sufficient in principle for a majority attack.

sources.title: Hash Power and the Limits of Law
sources.quote: Criminal and civil machinery connecting American courts to Chinese defendants is broken at every level... The formal law exists. The enforcement does not.

findings.analysis: The legal term R is load-bearing in the security model only where courts can reach, and his own geopolitical essay shows the reach failing for roughly half of global hash power — precisely the coalition he flags as majority-capable. The two essays are individually careful, but the strong claim ('every economically significant transaction') does not survive contact with his own enforcement map.
findings.resolution: Partial: the deterrence model also includes capital destruction (I) and coalition erosion (K), not only courts (R); and hash-power-and-the-limits-of-law proposes infrastructure chokepoints (DNS, BGP, relays) as non-judicial leverage. The residual gap — a state-shielded pool attacking a large transaction — is acknowledged by the policy proposals that close the essay.

findings.topic: 'Removes politics from money' vs 'blockchains relocate governance'

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: Fixing the protocol removes politics from money's foundation; code that cannot change is the only thing that resists money.

sources.title: The Necessity of the Stone: Protocol Finality, Political Intrusion, and the Integrity of Bitcoin
sources.quote: Fixing the fundamental rules... removes politics from money's foundation and creates the certainty that contracts, commerce and law require.

sources.title: Set in Stone or Sold to the Highest Bidder: Why Immutability Is Bitcoin's Only Defence
sources.quote: Code that cannot change is the only thing that resists money. If it bends, it will eventually kneel.

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: By 2026 the claim is relocation, not elimination: discretion moves to courts, regulators and surrounding institutions — there is no discretion-free zone.

sources.title: The Geography of Discretion
sources.quote: Constitutionalism never claimed to eliminate discretion, only to relocate it where it operates "slower, more public, more constrained by precedent"... The geography of discretion does not have a discretion-free zone marked on it.

sources.title: The Law of Controlled Amnesia
sources.quote: Blockchains do not abolish governance. They relocate it.

findings.analysis: The 2025 absolutist claim (immutability eliminates politics) is refined in 2026 into a constitutionalist claim (immutability relocates discretion to slower, more public venues). This is the corpus maturing under objection-handling rather than contradicting itself — but the earlier, stronger slogans are never retracted and continue to anchor the rhetoric.
findings.resolution: Self-supplied in the-geography-of-discretion, which answers the relocation objection directly and narrows the fixedness claim to the base layer: wire format, consensus rules and canonical ledger semantics.

findings.topic: 'Twenty-one million' — slogan repeated, then debunked

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: The issuance schedule is twenty-one million coins, written into code.

sources.title: The Necessity of the Stone: Protocol Finality, Political Intrusion, and the Integrity of Bitcoin
sources.quote: The issuance schedule — twenty-one million coins with halving intervals written into code.

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: There is no twenty-one million: the figure appears nowhere in the code and the true terminal supply is 20,999,999.9769.

sources.title: The Integer and the Idol
sources.quote: There are no decimals in Bitcoin. There is no twenty-one million.

sources.title: The Immutable Stock and the Unbounded Flow
sources.quote: The 21-million figure appears nowhere in the code; it emerges from the subsidy schedule.

findings.analysis: The earlier essay repeats the rounded slogan that the later essays mock as 'second-hander' arithmetic. Substantively harmless — the earlier sentence's point is that the schedule is coded, not that the literal constant exists — but it is a visible precision upgrade, and the later essays' tone (the slogan as idol) implicitly indicts his own earlier usage.
findings.resolution: The 2026 essays are themselves the correction; the earlier use is shorthand for the schedule.

findings.topic: 'Whoever controls the key controls the coins' vs the illusion-of-ownership essays

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: BSV's architecture reduces to a single proposition: key control is coin control.

sources.title: Cold Authority: Constructing an Air-Gapped Bitcoin SV Wallet Using ElectrumSV
sources.quote: The architecture of Bitcoin SV "reduces to a single proposition: whoever controls the private key controls the coins".

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: The keys-equals-coins slogan is an illusion: a key is evidence of control, never title, and under DAR even control fails (a frozen UTXO cannot be spent by its key-holder).

sources.title: Private Keys, Proofs, and the Illusion of Ownership in Digital Cash Systems
sources.quote: The slogan "if you hold the private keys, you own the coins" is an illusion. A private key is an instrument of access — the capability to sign — not a title of ownership.

sources.title: The Miner Is Not a Monarch
sources.quote: A private key is evidence of control. It is not metaphysical proof of indefeasible ownership.

findings.analysis: The wallet guide reaches for the folk slogan (in its control form) that the property essays dismantle, and it is strictly false under the corpus's own DAR framework, where a court order severs key control from coin control. Low stakes — the guide's context is operational security, not title — but it shows the slogan's gravitational pull even inside a corpus built to refute it.
findings.resolution: The control/ownership distinction itself: cold-authority is about custody practice, where 'control' is the operative goal; the law essays govern entitlement. Not acknowledged in the wallet essay.

findings.topic: One blockchain vs a competitive multi-currency CBDC ecosystem

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: The goal is explicitly not a single dominant system but open competition among many CBDCs and stablecoins interoperating via cross-chain communication.

sources.title: The Future of Digital Currency: The Need for Global Competition in CBDCs and Stablecoins
sources.quote: The goal should not be to create a single, dominant system controlled by one or a few entities, but rather to encourage open, competitive markets for digital currencies.

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: There can only be one blockchain; multi-chain fragmentation is an artificial tax and cross-chain bridges are rent-extracting toll booths.

sources.title: The Graveyard of Gateways: Why There Can Only Be One Blockchain
sources.quote: If one chain verifiably delivers the relevant functionality more cheaply at scale, fragmentation is an artificial tax, not diversity... Every boundary is a fee. Every crossing is a risk. Every bridge is an intermediary.

findings.analysis: The 2025 essay's 'cross-chain communication' and anti-single-system language collides with the 2026 one-chain thesis and its bridge graveyard. The charitable reading — many currencies issued as tokens on one scalable substrate — reconciles most of it, and the CBDC essay's own 'unified, interoperable blockchain ecosystem' phrase supports that reading; but the earlier essay's explicit rejection of 'a single, dominant system' is hard to square with 'there can only be one blockchain'.
findings.resolution: Implicit: competition among currencies on one shared ledger (the digest's own gloss of the CBDC essay is "many currencies on one scalable, interoperable substrate"). The one-chain essay states its conclusion conditionally ("if one chain verifiably delivers..."), leaving room for the competition that matters to be the contest to become the standard.

findings.topic: Off-chain channels: endorsed scaling mechanism vs subtraction from the security budget

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: Moving transactions off-chain into payment channels starves the fee base that must replace the halving subsidy; the more successful the layer, the smaller the security budget protecting it.

sources.title: The Defence That Halves
sources.quote: Every transaction successfully moved off-chain is a subtraction from the fee base that was supposed to replace the subsidy.

sources.title: Lightning's Velvet Manacles: Watchtowers, Custody, and the Quiet Return of Shadow Banking
sources.quote: Lightning's outcome is not corruption of design; it is the design, unfolding without deviation.

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: Hash chains, payment channels and blind e-cash that settle to the chain only twice per million payments are the endorsed architecture that makes a fixed monetary base economically tolerable — and Craig ships his own bonded channel implementation.

sources.title: The Immutable Stock and the Unbounded Flow
sources.quote: A channel that processes a million updates writes twice to the chain — once to open, once to close.

sources.title: Selling the Unspent Chain
sources.quote: Across the chain's whole life the ledger records two events — channel open and channel close.

sources.title: The Builder's Week: A Working Bitcoin Stack Appears, One Repository at a Time
sources.quote: bonded-subsat-channel: the user chooses a granularity k (k = 1,000,000 gives millionth-of-a-satoshi micro-units, off-chain only)

findings.analysis: The fee-subtraction argument in 'The Defence That Halves' is mechanism-independent: a channel transaction is 'a fee that never reaches a miner while the value moved still rests on base-layer security'. That is exactly the structure Craig celebrates and builds for BSV (two on-chain writes per million off-chain payments). If channels starve security on BTC, the same arithmetic applies to his own channel stack on BSV, which runs the identical halving schedule; if channels are fine on BSV because the base scales, the BTC critique loses its generality. The valence attached to the identical mechanism flips depending on which chain is being discussed.
findings.resolution: Partial only. 'The Builder's Week' distinguishes his bonded design from Lightning technically (one-satoshi bond instead of a penalty branch, since CLTV/CSV are no-ops on post-Genesis BSV), which answers the custody/penalty critique — but no essay addresses the fee-base subtraction that 'The Defence That Halves' makes the load-bearing argument against BTC.

findings.topic: The flow-cost security identity is wielded against BTC but never applied to BSV's own present-day budget

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: A chain's defence equals what miners are paid right now; aggregate miner expenditure equals aggregate revenue, so halve revenue and you halve rewrite cost — a chain without a large fee market becomes cheaper to rewrite on every plausible price path.

sources.title: The Defence That Halves
sources.quote: A chain that will not scale cannot fund its own defence. The arithmetic sets the rate.

sources.title: The Asset That Pays Rent to Exist
sources.quote: BTC is a flow — a service that must be re-purchased from the physical world continuously, block after block, at a price the protocol pins directly to the market price of the asset itself.

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: BSV is presented as the working, secure global digital cash today — yet its current fee revenue (penny-class fees at modest volume) is a small fraction of BTC's, and the corpus's own population-problem result concedes small-revenue chains sit in the formally unsafe region.

sources.title: Bitcoin Has a Population Problem — And We Can Prove It
sources.quote: Small PoW chains with B in the tens of thousands of dollars may have n* in single digits — the margin region 'is the operating regime'.

sources.title: Bitcoin After the Casino
sources.quote: the sustainable model is 'high volume multiplied by low fees'

findings.analysis: The security-equals-current-revenue identity is chain-agnostic, and by the corpus's own fee audit BSV's present fee base is far smaller than BTC's; applied even-handedly, the identity predicts BSV's rewrite cost today is very low. No essay applies the Defence-That-Halves arithmetic to BSV's present, only to BTC's future — an asymmetry of application that the whole security-economics cluster depends on. Craig's escape routes (future volume; legal deterrence) are argued generically, not quantified for BSV now.
findings.resolution: Partial. 'The Law Already Inside Bitcoin' (2026-03-17) supplies a second, non-flow security regime — 'Bitcoin's security does not depend on being beyond the law. It depends on being embedded in it.' — and the population-problem essay's concession about small chains is the closest the corpus comes to acknowledging the point.

findings.topic: Fee-dominant revenue is both the prescribed end-state and, in his own simulations, the destabilising regime

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: Bitcoin's designed and sustainable end-state is a fee-dominant revenue regime: the subsidy was scaffolding, the fee market the building — high volume multiplied by low fees.

sources.title: The Defence That Halves
sources.quote: The subsidy was scaffolding. The fee market was the building.

sources.title: The Priesthood of Artificial Scarcity
sources.quote: Mining economics admit only two equilibria as the subsidy halves: massive transaction volume at low fees, or tiny volume at extremely high fees.

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: His own repeated-mining-game simulations find fee-dominant regimes are deviation-dominant in 93.75% of runs even at low fee volatility, and 100% oscillatory at high volatility — while subsidy-anchored regimes converge to cooperation.

sources.title: The Nash Equilibrium in Digital Cash Systems
sources.quote: Fee-dominant regimes (κ = 0.10–0.30) are deviation-dominant in 93.75% of runs even at low fee volatility (σ_f 0.00–0.10).

findings.analysis: Every chain on the original schedule — BSV included — is driven toward fee dominance as the subsidy halves, and Craig insists this transition is the design's intent. Yet his own simulation paper reports that fee dominance, not volatility alone, destroys cooperative convergence: the result holds 'even at low fee volatility', which closes the obvious reconciliation that BSV's stable low fees behave differently. Either the simulation's parameterisation secretly encodes BTC-like congestion (in which case it proves less than claimed), or the prescribed end-state for Bitcoin is one his own model shows to be deviation-dominant.
findings.resolution: Null in the corpus. The Nash essay notes 'Subsidy enlarges the cooperative basin; it does not abolish the mechanism', but no essay reconciles the fee-dominant end-state he prescribes with the fee-dominant instability he measures.

findings.topic: The Huberman et al. fee theory he cites against BTC is capacity-generic and so cuts against his own high-volume-low-fee security model

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: Citing Huberman, Leshno & Moallemi (2021): fee revenue is bounded because fees price delay, not value secured — revenue 'depends only on K, ρ, and the distribution of delay costs F... and therefore does not depend on the exchange rate', and congestion is an inefficient tax base at every block size (Theorem 7).

sources.title: The Asset That Pays Rent to Exist
sources.quote: The thermostat is not merely weak. It is not wired to anything.

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: BSV's security model is explicitly volume times low fees — a billion transactions at $0.0001 each yielding $100,000 per block — which presupposes a fee market that can fund security without congestion.

sources.title: Why Transaction Throughput Determines How Long Bitcoin's Security Model Holds
sources.quote: a billion transactions at $0.0001 each yields $100,000 per block without pricing anyone out

sources.title: Bitcoin After the Casino
sources.quote: the sustainable model is 'high volume multiplied by low fees'

findings.analysis: The imported impossibility result is block-size-generic: if fees price delay, then on an uncongested elastic-capacity chain there is no delay to price, and fee revenue tends toward the marginal cost floor rather than toward any function of value secured. Craig uses the paper to show BTC's fee market cannot replace the subsidy, then assumes a fee market of the same theoretical type can replace it on BSV given enough volume. The volume answer may work arithmetically, but the cited theory denies the feedback loop his model needs — security demand never bids fees up on either chain.
findings.resolution: Partial. The same essay notes Huberman et al.'s own prescription is elastic capacity ('consonant with Wright's unbounded-block position'), and the legal-deterrence essays supply a non-fee security term; but the fee-theory asymmetry itself is never addressed.

findings.topic: The corpus's own fee figures span six orders of magnitude, and the nano-economy precondition ('no batching, finality at the core') contradicts the audit's batching prescription

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: BSV's penny-anchored fee is what makes micropayments viable — 'when they anchor at $0.01, they scale' — and tiny tickets must be batched (N > 10) to keep fee share under 5%.

sources.title: Digital Cash That Doesn't Bleed: A 11,000-Transaction Micropayment Audit Across PayPal, Stripe, Visa, Mastercard, and BSV
sources.quote: staying below 5% requires N > 10, and N = 20 yields 2.5% — enabling honest per-event metering with per-session settlement

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: The nano-economy requires per-act settlement cheaper than the act itself (acts priced at 0.0001¢–0.01¢), such systems 'do not tolerate batching, reversibility, or float', and later essays model fees of $0.0001, $0.00003 and a production cost floor of $0.00000002.

sources.title: The Dawn of the Nano-Economy: New Frontiers Unlocked by Sub-Cent Micropayments
sources.quote: Such systems 'do not tolerate batching, reversibility, or float. They require finality at their core.'

sources.title: When the Tollkeepers Disappear: The Consequences of Real Digital Cash
sources.quote: at fees as low as $0.00003, pay-per-use services, granular content monetisation, machine-to-machine transactions and real-time dynamic pricing become operational

sources.title: When Money Moves for Free, Who Gets Paid?
sources.quote: The benchmarked floor for cryptographic settlement on scalable blockchain infrastructure is ~$0.00000002 per transaction

findings.analysis: A $0.01 anchored fee is 10,000× the value of a 0.0001¢ sensor reading and 500,000× the stated cost floor; the audit's own arithmetic concedes a single 2p call at a 1p fee is a 50% share. The celebrated 'penny anchor' is viable only for payments above roughly $0.20, which excludes the entire nano-economy the corpus promises — unless payments are batched or channelled, which the nano-economy essay expressly rules out ('do not tolerate batching... finality at their core'). The figures are presented in different registers (measured fee, modelled fee, cost floor), but no essay reconciles them into one fee schedule.
findings.resolution: Partial. The audit essay itself supplies 'per-event metering with per-session settlement', and the channel essays supply the amortisation mechanism — but adopting that reconciliation concedes the nano-economy's stated precondition of per-act, unbatched finality.

findings.topic: By his own rent definition, the gap between the $0.00000002 cost floor and the $0.01 anchored fee is a 500,000× 'structural wedge'

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: A structural wedge between the cost of producing something and the price charged for it is economic rent; the cost of producing trusted transfer collapses to a floor near $0.00000002 per transaction.

sources.title: When Money Moves for Free, Who Gets Paid?
sources.quote: Where you find a structural wedge between the cost of producing something and the price charged for it, you have found economic rent.

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: BSV's fee is anchored at roughly $0.01 and celebrated as the viable end-state for micropayments.

sources.title: Digital Cash That Doesn't Bleed: A 11,000-Transaction Micropayment Audit Across PayPal, Stripe, Visa, Mastercard, and BSV
sources.quote: BSV's flat, penny-class fee (anchored at roughly $0.01) never breaches 5%

findings.analysis: The two essays use different quantities (production cost floor versus charged fee), so this is not a numeric contradiction; the tension is that the corpus's rent-detection instrument, applied to its own favoured rail, returns a wedge of five orders of magnitude. Craig would presumably answer that the wedge is the security budget, not rent — but that identification (fee minus cost equals defence expenditure) is exactly the move his rent framework denies to banks and card networks.
findings.resolution: Partial. The floor is expressly 'a floor, not a production figure', and 'The Defence That Halves' frames all miner revenue as defence expenditure; the two framings are never placed side by side.

findings.topic: Fixed supply: the lever that removes politics from money vs the supply rule that implies no discipline at all

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: Fixing the issuance schedule and supply 'eliminated that lever' of political manipulation and breaks the historical cycle in which every money was corrupted by politics; permanence is honesty is value.

sources.title: The Necessity of the Stone: Protocol Finality, Political Intrusion, and the Integrity of Bitcoin
sources.quote: In the stone lies its permanence. In permanence lies its honesty. And in honesty lies its value.

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: A fixed supply neither restrains states nor disciplines the system built on it: scarcity without elasticity is paralysis, a deflationary unit 'would turn every recession into a depression', and fixed supply implies proliferating off-chain abstractions, not discipline.

sources.title: The Myth of the Bitcoin Standard: Debt, Delusion, and the Enduring Economics of State Spending
sources.quote: Gold failed because it assumed men could be governed by metal. Bitcoin will fail because it assumes men can be governed by code.

sources.title: The Mirage of the Bitcoin Standard: Fractional Reserve Finance in Digital Form
sources.quote: Fixed supply does not imply fixed discipline; it implies the proliferation of abstractions

findings.analysis: Written one month apart, the October essay celebrates the fixed supply as the definitive break with political money while the November essays deny that any supply rule can discipline political behaviour or prevent shadow elasticity. The charitable reading — the stone constrains base issuance, not the credit superstructure or the state's borrowing — is available and partially supplied ('Scarcity, under the banner of virtue, births elasticity in the shadows'), but the normative valence of inelasticity itself flips: 'the most explicit defiance of political tradition' versus 'a nightmare of inelastic despair'.
findings.resolution: Partial. The base-versus-superstructure distinction is implicit across the two Bitcoin-Standard essays; 'The Immutable Stock and the Unbounded Flow' later adds the stock/flow decoupling that would let a capped base coexist with elastic payments.

findings.topic: 'Twenty-one million coins... written into code' vs 'There is no twenty-one million'

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: The issuance schedule — twenty-one million coins with halving intervals — is written into the code as part of Bitcoin's sealed constitution.

sources.title: The Necessity of the Stone: Protocol Finality, Political Intrusion, and the Integrity of Bitcoin
sources.quote: What was sealed: the structure of transactions, signature validation, conditions of block acceptance, proof-of-work rules, and the issuance schedule — twenty-one million coins with halving intervals written into code.

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: The 21-million figure appears nowhere in the code and is arithmetically false: the truncating right-shift yields exactly 20,999,999.9769 coins.

sources.title: The Integer and the Idol
sources.quote: There are no decimals in Bitcoin. There is no twenty-one million.

sources.title: The Immutable Stock and the Unbounded Flow
sources.quote: The 21-million figure appears nowhere in the code; it emerges from the subsidy schedule

findings.analysis: A clean factual contradiction between the October 2025 essay (21M written into code) and the May 2026 essays (the figure is nowhere in the code and is a 'rounded-up slogan'). The substantive stakes are tiny (a 0.0231-coin shortfall) and the deeper claim — a fixed, inception-defined supply — is shared, so this reads as the corpus correcting its own shorthand over time rather than a worldview clash.
findings.resolution: Yes, by supersession: the later essays supply the exact sum (2,099,999,997,690,000 satoshis) and explicitly recast the round figure as a slogan; 'The Forked Illusion' (2025-12-07) had already mocked elevating '21 million' to 'a cosmic decree'.

findings.topic: Prices: Hayekian compressed knowledge vs a barometer of collective arousal

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: The price system is a communication system that compresses dispersed scarcity signals into actionable form — the Hayekian foundation of his intermediation and transaction-cost economics.

sources.title: The Economy Has Always Been Data
sources.quote: The price system is primarily a communication system that compresses scarcity signals into actionable form.

sources.title: The Toll Booth Economy
sources.quote: prices are compressed signals that coordinate it

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: The market is not an information system at all; price is a barometer of tension, not truth — aggregated emotion mistaken for guidance.

sources.title: Ventriloquising the Void: How Economies Pretend to Speak
sources.quote: Price, then, is not a measure of worth but of collective arousal. It is a barometer of tension, not truth.

findings.analysis: The November 2025 essay states in full generality that 'What society calls "the market" is not an information system but a psychological prosthesis'; the May–June 2026 essays build his entire anti-intermediation economics on the Hayekian premise that prices are compressed knowledge which intermediaries corrupt. Both cannot be the corpus's default theory of price. The obvious reconciliation — speculative crypto markets are ritual while goods markets are informative — is never stated, and the rent-wedge and fee-geometry arguments elsewhere treat market prices as evidentiary.
findings.resolution: Null. The ventriloquism essay's targets are crypto markets, but its claims are framed about 'the market' as such, and no essay draws the speculative/productive distinction explicitly.

findings.topic: Instant settlement: a necessity for global trade vs 'the wrong margin' that removes at most a few per cent

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: Instant, final settlement is a defining property of real digital cash and a necessity for global trade; banks monetise settlement dead time, and instant settlement reduces credit-line needs, capital requirements and settlement risk.

sources.title: The Future of Digital Currency: The Need for Global Competition in CBDCs and Stablecoins
sources.quote: This shift toward instantaneous cross-border payments is not just a luxury but a necessity for the future of global trade.

sources.title: When the Tollkeepers Disappear: The Consequences of Real Digital Cash
sources.quote: Instant settlement reduces credit-line needs, lowers capital requirements and eliminates settlement risk.

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: In large-value trade, settlement latency is not a meaningful cost: working capital is locked in the 45–110-day receivables cycle, faster finality removes at most low single digits of carry, and rails do not shorten negotiated terms by one minute.

sources.title: Settlement Speed Is the Wrong Margin
sources.quote: The people selling milliseconds are solving a problem these firms do not have.

findings.analysis: The June 2026 measurement essay refutes, with firm-level data, precisely the mechanism ('settlement dead time' monetised by banks; credit-line needs reduced by instant settlement) that the March and April 2026 essays assert as benefits and the June 2025 essay calls a necessity. Because the sweeping version persists into April 2026, this is not a clean evolution; it is a live tension between the polemical and empirical registers. The later essay's own carve-out (in machine-to-machine payments T falls toward L and 'finality is the holding period') confines the speed thesis to the micropayment regime.
findings.resolution: Partial, supplied by the later essay itself: the λ = L/T framework makes speed decisive only where the holding period is the latency (machine payments), implicitly retracting the trade-credit version of the claim.

findings.topic: 'Transactions, once made, are final' vs 'settlement is probabilistic; genuine finality is a legal object'

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: Real digital cash delivers instant settlement final within seconds; transactions, once made, are final; nano-payments are permanent and irrevocable.

sources.title: When the Tollkeepers Disappear: The Consequences of Real Digital Cash
sources.quote: Transactions, once made, are final. Access is not contingent on approval.

sources.title: The Dawn of the Nano-Economy: New Frontiers Unlocked by Sub-Cent Micropayments
sources.quote: It is verified action + irreversible payment = concluded transaction.

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: Consensus settlement is only ever probabilistic; a payment in an orphaned block 'did not, in the end, happen', and genuine finality is a legal commitment only a recognising legal order has ever supplied.

sources.title: The Dial That Used to Be Fixed
sources.quote: Settlement is probabilistic, subject to fork and reorganisation; a payment in an orphaned block 'did not, in the end, happen'.

sources.title: Nobody Asks Where Your Banknote Has Been
sources.quote: Against 'blockchain payments are final': the sentence is not a proposition but a question — final in which of the four senses?

findings.analysis: The payments essays promise protocol-delivered finality in seconds as a system property; the law-and-money essays of the same summer deny that any blockchain delivers finality at all, resolving 'final' into four distinct senses of which only the operational one is technical. The two bodies of work are individually careful but rhetorically incompatible: 'final within seconds' is, by the later framework, a category error. The four-finalities apparatus and the two-regime security model (protocol for small payments, law for large) supply the reconciliation — at the cost of the earlier slogans.
findings.resolution: Partial. The later essays' own framework (operational finality for small payments; legal finality above) reconciles the substance, and 'The Law Already Inside Bitcoin' supplies the two-regime structure; the earlier absolute phrasing is never expressly qualified.

findings.topic: Coase: near-zero transaction costs dissolve the firm vs mining firms as Coase's theory running in fast-forward

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: As transaction costs fall toward zero, 'the logic of the firm starts to crumble' — micropayments plus immutable proof undermine the Coasean rationale for firms, hierarchies and intermediaries.

sources.title: Micropayments, Immutable Data, and the Economic Revolution of Near-Zero Transaction Costs
sources.quote: As transaction costs fall toward zero, 'the logic of the firm starts to crumble' and decentralised market coordination becomes superior to hierarchy.

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: Even in an environment stripped of historical baggage, firms emerge inevitably from cost structure: mining consolidation into vertically integrated corporations is Coase's 1937 theory playing out in fast-forward.

sources.title: Why Bitcoin Miners Form Companies: What Blockchain Teaches Us About the Nature of Firms
sources.quote: Mining consolidation isn't a pathology. It's Coase's theory of the firm, running in fast-forward, in an environment stripped of all the historical baggage

findings.analysis: The July 2025 essay drives the friction term to zero and derives the dissolution of hierarchy; the February 2026 essay shows firms forming in the one industry closest to that condition, because organisational costs, revenue variance and asset specificity survive even when market transaction costs collapse. The reconciliation is orthodox Coase (the margin moves, the firm does not vanish) and is implicit in the later essay's three-cost-force model — but the earlier essay's sweeping 'crumble' claim needs that qualification and does not contain it.
findings.resolution: Partial. 'Who Shall Keep the Keys?' (2026-06-03) supplies the mature version — 'the firm (a redrawn boundary and redistributed trust-rents)' — which is the qualified claim both essays can support.

findings.topic: Proof-of-work energy: the cost of governance legitimacy vs watts burned to buy scarcity

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: PoW energy expenditure is not waste; it is the institutional cost of producing governance legitimacy under permissionless constraints, analogous to the administrative costs of elections and courts.

sources.title: Why Bitcoin Miners Form Companies: What Blockchain Teaches Us About the Nature of Firms
sources.quote: Energy expenditure in proof of work isn't waste—it's the cost of producing governance legitimacy under the constraints of a permissionless system.

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: BTC's energy burn is parasitism: mining consumes productive inputs to maintain an inert scarcity token; the energy is not buying throughput, it is buying scarcity.

sources.title: The Cult of Scarcity
sources.quote: The energy is not buying throughput; it is buying scarcity.

sources.title: The Cult of Scarcity
sources.quote: mining 'consumes productive inputs to maintain an inert scarcity token'

findings.analysis: Both claims are about proof-of-work as such, and their flat wordings ('isn't waste' versus 'economic cannibalism') collide. The corpus's consistent underlying frame — energy divided by useful throughput is the metric — reconciles them: the same joule is legitimacy on a chain carrying commerce and waste on a five-TPS chain. But that denominator argument has to be assembled by the reader; the essays as written contradict in valence.
findings.resolution: Yes, in substance: 'The Defence That Halves' unifies the two — 'The electricity is what leaves the system. The security is what it was meant to purchase.' — making utility-per-joule the consistent criterion.

findings.topic: One week in August 2025: micropayments and SPV as dystopian enclosure vs as liberation and the only road worth walking

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: Micropayment culture encloses the commons — every interaction priced, metered and billed, dovetailing with behavioural scoring and social-credit architectures — and SPV is 'a delegation of trust dressed as independence'.

sources.title: Mechanised Myths: Control, Compliance, and the Dystopian Present
sources.quote: Micropayment culture encloses the commons: every interaction priced, metered and billed, dovetailing with behavioural scoring, social-credit architectures and the gamification of compliance

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: Micropayments are an insurgency that breaks corporate siege and operationalises moral stewardship, and SPV is the cornerstone of the peer-to-peer design.

sources.title: Pennies and Power: How Micropayments Could Break the Corporate Siege
sources.quote: Frictionless micropayments are not a feature but an insurgency.

sources.title: A Mechanism of Honour - Ledger of Blood and Electricity
sources.quote: SPV is 'not merely a shortcut—it is the only road worth walking'

findings.analysis: Within ten days the corpus deploys the same two technologies as dystopian instruments of compliance (5 August) and as emancipation (30 July, 9–10 August). The summary of 'Mechanised Myths' itself flags the SPV usage as sitting 'in tension with Craig's usual technical defence of SPV'. The reconciliation — corporate, platform-owned micropayment rails enclose, while open-protocol micropayments liberate — is available from the essay's own 'in corporate hands' qualifier, but the allegorical use of SPV as outsourced truth contradicts his technical position outright.
findings.resolution: Partial. The dystopia essay's target is 'automation married to blockchain in corporate hands'; the summary notes the dark reading 'stands in creative tension' with the celebratory essays published days later.

findings.topic: Cross-chain communication: dismissed by name as unable to scale, then endorsed as the CBDC ecosystem's mechanism — three days apart

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: Sidechains, sharding and cross-chain communication cannot deliver the throughput global commerce demands; there is only one system that can scale, under a single overarching protocol.

sources.title: The Imperative of Scalable Blockchain for Global Commerce
sources.quote: Existing scaling approaches are dismissed by name: 'sidechains, sharding, and cross-chain communication' cannot deliver the millions of transactions per second that genuine global commerce demands

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: The future is a unified, interoperable ecosystem in which multiple CBDCs and stablecoins cooperate via cross-chain communication — and no single dominant system should exist.

sources.title: The Future of Digital Currency: The Need for Global Competition in CBDCs and Stablecoins
sources.quote: a unified, interoperable blockchain ecosystem in which multiple CBDCs and stablecoins cooperate via 'cross-chain communication'

findings.analysis: The 26 June essay dismisses 'cross-chain communication' by name and the 29 June essay makes it the connective tissue of the proposed monetary future; the later one-chain essay ('The Graveyard of Gateways', 2026-04-04: 'Every bridge is an intermediary') hardens the first position. The charitable reading — many currencies issued on one scalable ledger, with 'cross-chain' meaning cross-currency-system rather than cross-blockchain — reconciles the vision but not the words, and the 2025 essays give the reader no help.
findings.resolution: Partial. The tokenisation essays ('Stablecoins and the Lost Spark', 'The Cult of Digital Metallurgy') supply the one-ledger-many-currencies picture that reconciles the substance; the phrase-level contradiction stands.

findings.topic: Stablecoins: the most coherent actualisation of Satoshi's vision vs synthetic dollars masquerading as collateral

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: Stablecoins are not a deviation from Satoshi's vision but its most coherent actualisation; fiat backing is the spark that ignites adoption.

sources.title: Stablecoins and the Lost Spark
sources.quote: Where BTC Core erects a shrine, stablecoins build a marketplace.

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: Tether is the synthetic dollar masquerading as collateral, promising parity through mechanisms no one is allowed to see — part of the fractional-reserve illusion.

sources.title: Ghosts of Gold: Fractional Reserve Dynamics in the Age of BTC
sources.quote: Tether as 'the synthetic dollar masquerading as collateral', promising parity 'through mechanisms no one is allowed to see'

findings.analysis: Five weeks apart, the stablecoin concept is the fulfilment of the design and its largest instantiation is unmasked as opaque paper. Craig does supply the distinguishing line in the pro-stablecoin essay itself — USDT and USDC are 'primitive, permissioned instantiations' of an idea whose advanced forms include on-chain collateralisation — so the tension is between the concept and the incumbent, not between two incompatible theories. Still, the corpus never applies its own proof-of-reserves critique ('In Praise of Shadowled Ledgers') systematically to the instruments it praises.
findings.resolution: Yes, in principle: the concept-versus-instantiation distinction is stated in 'Stablecoins and the Lost Spark' itself.

findings.topic: Intermediation: a caste that produces nothing vs functions Craig himself defends as durable

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: Nearly forty per cent of global output — over US$40 trillion a year — is consumed by a financial intermediation sector that produces nothing.

sources.title: The Great Global Skim
sources.quote: more than US$40 trillion each year to a caste that produces nothing but movement without progress

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: Credit judgement, liquidity transformation and consumer protection are not settlement functions and survive; intermediaries are justified whenever they reduce the costs of exchange more than they increase dependency and rent.

sources.title: When Money Moves for Free, Who Gets Paid?
sources.quote: credit judgement, liquidity transformation and consumer protection are not settlement functions and survive

sources.title: The Toll Booth Economy
sources.quote: Intermediaries are justified only when they reduce the costs of exchange more than they increase dependency, delay, rent extraction and control

findings.analysis: The satirical register claims the entire intermediation sector 'produces nothing'; the analytical register explicitly rejects the 'blockchain replaces banks' maximalist claim and defends whole categories of financial function as durable and value-creating. The Skim essay also sums a flow (financial-sector GDP share) with a stock (shadow-banking assets) to reach its $40-trillion-a-year figure, which sits oddly beside the corpus's otherwise careful stock/flow discipline. The maximalist rhetoric is the outlier, but it is the quoted, dramatised version of the thesis (it recurs in 'The Coin That Must Never Rise').
findings.resolution: Partial. The careful essays supply the rent-versus-service distinction that the Skim collapses; no essay reconciles the 40%/$40T headline with the defended functions.

findings.topic: Scarcity: a fetish and a cult vs Bitcoin's deeper achievement

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: Engineered scarcity is a morally perverse cult: the 21-million cap is 'a myth of engineered scarcity', scarcity is 'a fetish, a sacralised austerity masquerading as wisdom'.

sources.title: "Where Your Treasure Is": A Christian Denunciation of Hoarding, HODL Culture, and False Promises of Wealth Without Work
sources.quote: The 21-million cap is 'a myth of engineered scarcity'

sources.title: The Great Global Skim
sources.quote: BTC's scarcity is 'a fetish, a sacralised austerity masquerading as wisdom'

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: Digital scarcity is Bitcoin's deeper achievement and one of the two capabilities that touch the load-bearing walls of the social order.

sources.title: Bitcoin After the Casino
sources.quote: Its deeper achievement is digital scarcity at the level of individual transactions

sources.title: Who Shall Keep the Keys?
sources.quote: Trustless coordination and engineered digital scarcity touch the load-bearing walls of the social order

findings.analysis: The same word carries opposite valences depending on whether the target is the supply cap as speculative theology (attacked) or unique, un-copyable digital states as property infrastructure (praised). Craig supplies the distinction himself — 'Scarcity is not merely 21 million: transactional scarcity... Ownership moves rather than multiplies' — so this is an emphasis shift rather than a contradiction, but a reader of only the anti-scarcity essays would be surprised by the pro-scarcity ones.
findings.resolution: Yes: 'Bitcoin After the Casino' explicitly distinguishes transactional scarcity (unique spendable states) from the supply-cap cult.

findings.topic: Hoarding condemned as rot vs 'save all you can' praised as capitalism's moral spine

position_a.label: Position A
position_a.claim: HODL culture is vice: passive speculation is the burial of talent, and to hoard is to rot.

sources.title: "Where Your Treasure Is": A Christian Denunciation of Hoarding, HODL Culture, and False Promises of Wealth Without Work
sources.quote: To hold, in the true Biblical sense, is to steward. To hoard is to rot.

position_b.label: Position B
position_b.claim: Wesley's triad — gain all you can, save all you can, give all you can — is capitalism's moral spine, with saving as anti-waste reinvestment.

sources.title: Stewardship in the Smallest Coin: Wesleyan Capitalism and the Moral Economy of Micropayments
sources.quote: Gain all you can, save all you can, give all you can.

findings.analysis: Seven weeks apart, holding wealth is condemned and saving is blessed. The essays themselves supply the distinction — 'save is anti-waste reinvestment', whereas HODL is idle appreciation-seeking — and the later custody essay ('Digital Cash Is Not a Vault': 'Digital savings need the security of savings') confirms that saving, as opposed to speculative hoarding, is legitimate in his framework. This is an emphasis difference with an in-corpus reconciliation, not a contradiction.
findings.resolution: Yes: the stewardship essay defines 'save' as anti-waste reinvestment, and 'Digital Cash Is Not a Vault' (2026-08-12) institutionalises the spending/saving distinction.

findings.topic: 'Decentralized' / 'censorship resistant' as unquantified marketing adjectives

position_a.label: BRC llm-training-guide
position_a.claim: UHRP downloads are described as 'Censorship resistant (no central control)'; overlays are 'Decentralized indexing infrastructure'; IdentityClient 'queries decentralized identity resolution services' under the heading 'Decentralized identity attestation'. No metric, threshold or failure model is attached to any of these adjectives.
position_a.section: Section 5 'Decentralized Resolution' (~line 607); Section 6 'Overlay Architecture' (~line 672); Section 3 'Identity System Architecture' (~lines 180-186)

position_b.label: Craig Wright corpus
position_b.claim: Decentralisation claims are worthless unless measurable, and 'censorship resistance' has a specific structural meaning — no non-miner can prevent the inclusion of a fee-paying transaction — not a vague aura of having no obvious centre.

sources.title: Decentralization Deserves a Number
sources.quote: Counting nodes tells you almost nothing. Measuring cross-layer separability tells you a great deal.

sources.title: Effective Decentralisation Is the Minimum, Not the Average
sources.quote: Decentralisation is reported as a number. It is not a number. It is a vector.

sources.title: The Two Tiers Are a Market, Not a Cage
sources.quote: Censorship resistance is the structural property that no non-miner can prevent the inclusion of a fee-paying transaction.

findings.analysis: The guide's adjectives are exactly the unquantified rhetoric Craig's measurement essays attack, and his censorship-resistance definition is about miner inclusion of transactions, not file-storage availability — a UHRP provider can still refuse to host or serve a file, so the claim overstates the architecture. Not a flat contradiction because the guide's described mechanics (multiple lookup services, failover to alternative hosts, multiple storage providers, multiple overlays tracking the same transaction) are substitutable-service design, which is materially closer to his operational tests than the vocabulary suggests. The gap is between the marketing adjective and the engineering underneath it.

findings.topic: Centralised message boxes and trusted certifiers vs the anti-toll-booth critique

position_a.label: BRC llm-training-guide
position_a.claim: Message boxes are 'Centralized servers (easy to deploy)' providing 'Server-hosted relay infrastructure' for store-and-forward messaging; certificates come from a 'Certifier: trusted authority issuing certificates' at a hardcoded host ('https://message-box-us-1.bsvb.tech', 'https://certify.bsvb.tech').
position_a.section: Section 12 'Message Box Architecture' (~lines 1730-1734); Section 7 (~line 917); Section 8 'Acquire Certificates from Certifiers' (~lines 1090-1113)

position_b.label: Craig Wright corpus
position_b.claim: Intermediaries are condemned when they are compulsory toll booths, not when they are optional, substitutable service providers paid for a task — the line is necessity and non-substitutability, not existence.

sources.title: The Toll Booth Economy
sources.quote: Intermediaries are justified only when they reduce the costs of exchange more than they increase dependency, delay, rent extraction and control.

sources.title: The Protocol No Gatekeeper Wants
sources.quote: If a service disappears, can another service recover and continue the relationship from evidence controlled by the parties? If the answer is no, the system remains centralised at the point that matters.

sources.title: The Protocol No Gatekeeper Wants
