sources.quote: The service remains useful. It ceases to be sovereign.

findings.analysis: This answers the optional-vs-necessary question directly: Craig permits intermediaries that fail to become gatekeepers. The guide's message box is optional (Section 9 lists overlays, UHRP or a database as alternatives), end-to-end encrypted so the server 'cannot read message contents', and host-parameterised — a service provider, not a toll booth; the certifier attests but never custodies, matching his 'certifier of fact, not keeper of records' model. The residual tension is practical rather than philosophical: the documented defaults hardcode single bsvb.tech hosts, and under his substitutability test a deployment with one live provider 'remains centralised at the point that matters' regardless of how replaceable the protocol makes it in principle.

findings.topic: 'Identity key represents user identity' vs keys are control, not identity

position_a.label: BRC llm-training-guide
position_a.claim: 'identityKey: true retrieves the master identity key'; 'Public key is safe to share (represents user identity)'; 'Identity keys are deterministic (same key every time)' — a persistent master key presented as the user's identity, resolvable by attributes through identity services.
position_a.section: Section 3 'Derive Identity Keys from Wallet' (~lines 198-207) and 'Resolve Identity Keys by Attributes' (~lines 180-189)

position_b.label: Craig Wright corpus
position_b.claim: A key proves control of a key and nothing more; binding a key to a person requires attestation evidence from outside the chain, and treating a persistent key as a person's identity inverts the evidentiary order.

sources.title: The Gospel According to Grok
sources.quote: Possession of a key proves possession of a key.

sources.title: The Gospel According to Grok
sources.quote: The blockchain records transactions, not identity; a signature proves control of a key and nothing more; and attributing a key to a person requires evidence from outside the chain.

sources.title: Private Keys, Proofs, and the Illusion of Ownership in Digital Cash Systems
sources.quote: The private key is not a title; it is an instrument of access.

sources.title: In Praise of Shadowled Ledgers: The Fiction of Proof Without Identity
sources.quote: A signature on a blockchain is not a deed. A wallet is not a safe. A key is not a name.

findings.analysis: The guide's vocabulary collapses precisely the control/identity distinction Craig repeatedly polices: a deterministic 'master identity key' that 'represents user identity' is the key-as-birth-certificate move he satirises in the Grok essay. The reconciliation is inside the guide itself — its certificate layer has a certifier verify claims out-of-band and then sign, which is exactly the external attestation Craig demands before a key may be tied to a person. Note also that Craig's own capability-first essay ('An account is not identity, it is an entry in someone else's ledger', 2025-08-23) supports key-proven capability as identity-in-transaction; what he rejects is the slide from capability to personhood and title, which is where the guide's phrasing, though not its architecture, carelessly goes.

findings.topic: PushDrop embeds data in on-chain locking scripts vs 'content off-chain'

position_a.label: BRC llm-training-guide
position_a.claim: 'PushDrop: token protocol with embedded data fields'; 'Embeds data directly in locking script. Fields are pushed onto the script stack' — arbitrary application data written into the chain itself inside 1-satoshi token outputs.
position_a.section: Section 6 'Create and Broadcast Tokens to Overlays' (~lines 656-666)

position_b.label: Craig Wright corpus
position_b.claim: The ledger tier is for small commitments whose meaning depends on when they were fixed; bulk content belongs in the off-chain content-addressed store — yet his own shipped code puts Merkle roots as pushdata inside live spendable scripts.

sources.title: Order On-Chain, Content Off-Chain, Judgement in the Overlay
sources.quote: Order on-chain. Content off-chain. Judgement in the overlay. And no hash has ever made anything true.

sources.title: Engraving in Stone: Encoding Images in Bitcoin (or BTC) Transactions
sources.quote: The ledger was never meant to be the world's scrapbook. It was meant to be its notary.

sources.title: The Builder's Week: A Working Bitcoin Stack Appears, One Repository at a Time
sources.quote: The Merkle root rides as pushdata in a live spendable script, never OP_RETURN, keeping evidence inside the chainable transaction graph.

findings.analysis: Superficially this collides with the content-off-chain rule, but Craig's own assignment test — commit whatever's meaning depends on when it was fixed — places token state on-chain, and his own verifiable-accounting repository embeds commitments as pushdata in spendable scripts, which is structurally what PushDrop does. The genuine constraint he imposes is economic and disciplined: small committed state on-chain, bulk bytes off-chain (which the guide honours by routing files through UHRP), and his 'Engraving in Stone' essay condemns raw bulk embedding as 'the permanence of landfill'. The tension reduces to a sizing rule: PushDrop is Craig-consistent while its fields stay small commitments, and drifts into his 'scrapbook' critique if applications stuff bulk content into locking scripts.

findings.topic: BEEF self-contained SPV validation vs Craig's SPV advocacy

position_a.label: BRC llm-training-guide
position_a.claim: BEEF 'is a transaction serialization format that includes input transaction history for SPV validation'; benefits include 'No blockchain queries needed (self-contained)', 'SPV validation without full node' and 'Deterministic validation (same result everywhere)'.
position_a.section: Section 9 'PATTERN: BEEF Transaction Format' (~lines 1277-1307); also Section 2 (~lines 104-106)

position_b.label: Craig Wright corpus
position_b.claim: SPV — headers, your own full input transactions and their Merkle paths — is the whitepaper's first-class verification model for ordinary users; proof, not universal redundancy, defines verification.

sources.title: Safe Low Bandwidth SPV: A Formal Treatment of Simplified Payment Verification Protocols and Security Bounds
sources.quote: SPV is not merely a means of saving bandwidth. It is a paradigm—a methodology that insists that proof, not redundancy, defines verification.

sources.title: A Mechanism of Honour - Ledger of Blood and Electricity
sources.quote: SPV is not merely a shortcut—it is the only road worth walking.

sources.title: The Cult of the Full Node
sources.quote: The proof travels with the value because value without proof is merely theatre.

findings.analysis: BEEF is the operational form of the exact SPV wallet contents Craig enumerates in 'A Mechanism of Honour' — full input transactions, their Merkle paths, optionally block headers — packaged so the proof travels with the value. The guide's claim that no blockchain queries or full node are needed is his 'proof, not redundancy' position stated as an API feature. This is the strongest single alignment between the guide and the corpus.

findings.topic: Overlay networks (TopicBroadcaster / LookupResolver) vs 'Judgement in the Overlay'

position_a.label: BRC llm-training-guide
position_a.claim: 'Overlay networks: topic-based transaction indexing'; 'Topic managers (tm_*) accept and index transactions'; 'Lookup services (ls_*) query indexed data'; 'Multiple overlays can track same transaction'; 'Topic managers validate and index'.
position_a.section: Section 6 'Overlay Architecture' (~lines 668-679) and 'Query Overlay Networks for Tokens' (~lines 714-718)

position_b.label: Craig Wright corpus
position_b.claim: Overlays are the designated tier for application-specific judgement over a common transaction substrate — revisable, competitive, and operable by anyone — separating protocol, database, identity, interface and governance.

sources.title: Order On-Chain, Content Off-Chain, Judgement in the Overlay
sources.quote: Anyone can run an overlay, and disagreement between two overlays over the same committed inputs is a well-formed dispute.

sources.title: The Protocol No Gatekeeper Wants
sources.quote: Overlays create application-specific views over a common transaction substrate, separating protocol, database, identity, interface and governance.

findings.analysis: The guide's tm_*/ls_* split — writers that validate and index versus readers that serve queries, with multiple overlays over the same transaction — is Craig's ledger/overlay separation in production clothing, and he has shipped an overlay-broadcast implementation of his own ('The Builder's Week', 2026-06-01). The architecture matches his model that the chain supplies ordering and evidence while judgement lives in replaceable, competing services.

findings.topic: UHRP content-addressed storage with paid retention vs the off-chain store tier

position_a.label: BRC llm-training-guide
position_a.claim: 'Hash of file is calculated. Availability advertised on blockchain (overlay network)... Anyone can retrieve using hash'; downloads 'Verify hash matches identifier'; 'retentionPeriod: temporary storage (pay per time)'; 'Multiple storage providers can host same file. Redundancy via multiple uploads'.

position_b.label: Craig Wright corpus
position_b.claim: The store tier is large, cheap and content-addressed — a corrupted copy is a detectably different object — needing availability rather than integrity, with hashes anchored on-chain and bulk bytes kept off-chain.

sources.title: Order On-Chain, Content Off-Chain, Judgement in the Overlay
sources.quote: The store is large and cheap, content-addressed so a corrupted copy is a detectably different object — it needs availability, not integrity.

sources.title: Engraving in Stone: Encoding Images in Bitcoin (or BTC) Transactions
sources.quote: You only need to store the right bytes.

findings.analysis: UHRP is close to a literal instantiation of Craig's middle tier: content addressed by SHA-256 hash, integrity enforced by hash verification at download, availability sold as a metered service (paid retention periods), and redundancy achieved by engaging multiple competing providers rather than by trusting one. The on-chain component is only the hash-bearing advertisement — precisely the 'hashes going up' join his capstone describes.

findings.topic: BRC-29 per-payment ECDH key derivation vs Craig's IP-to-IP notes protocol

position_a.label: BRC llm-training-guide
position_a.claim: BRC-29 derives payment keys from the recipient's identity key plus a per-payment keyID via shared-secret derivation: 'Generates unique keys per transaction for privacy', 'No key reuse (enhanced privacy)', 'Counterparty-specific (different keys per recipient)', with funds locked to standard P2PKH addresses.
position_a.section: Section 3 'BRC-29 Protocol' (~lines 219-230); Section 4 'Payment Privacy Architecture' (~lines 271-275); Section 11 (~lines 1689-1706)

position_b.label: Craig Wright corpus
position_b.claim: His own published wallet protocol derives per-payment P2PKH keys from an ECDH shared element between the parties' identity keys, with identity keys authenticating the off-chain channel and never appearing on-chain.

sources.title: IP-to-IP Negotiated Notes: An ECDH-Derived, Multi-Transfer Wallet Protocol for Private, Settled Digital-Cash Payments
sources.quote: Identity keys are used only for ECDH and message authentication; they never appear on-chain.

sources.title: Censorship Resistance, Atomic Settlement, and the Limits of Coalition Power
sources.quote: The protocol's native mode is atomic settlement with fresh single-use keypairs (section 10 of the white paper).

findings.analysis: BRC-29 is the same construction family Craig specifies: ECDH between identity keys, deterministic per-payment child keys that only the recipient can spend from, standard P2PKH outputs, no new opcodes or gadgets. The guide's privacy rationale (no address reuse, counterparty-specific keys defeating graph analysis) restates the whitepaper's section-10 key-reuse model that Craig's censorship essay calls the protocol's native mode.

findings.topic: Certifier-signed certificates with selective disclosure vs Craig's identity framework

position_a.label: BRC llm-training-guide
position_a.claim: 'Certifier verifies subject's claims (out-of-band)' then signs a certificate whose fields are 'Encrypted by default (privacy-preserving)' with 'Subject controls field disclosure'; verifiable presentations use verifier-specific keyrings so the verifier 'cannot decrypt unrevealed fields'.
position_a.section: Section 8 'Certificate Architecture' (~lines 1118-1135) and 'Create Verifiable Certificates with Selective Disclosure' (~lines 1238-1263)

position_b.label: Craig Wright corpus
position_b.claim: Identity should be holder-custodied verifiable credentials: the issuer (state or otherwise) attests to facts at issuance and then withdraws, with zero-knowledge or attribute-based selective disclosure to verifiers.

sources.title: Digital Identity and the Architecture of Autonomy: A Framework for Self-Sovereign Verification in a Stateless System
sources.quote: The government becomes a certifier of fact, not a keeper of records.

sources.title: The Mark That Belongs to No One
sources.quote: A signature may be anything. But it must be someone's.

findings.analysis: The guide's certificate stack is Craig's issuer-holder-verifier triad implemented: attestation happens out-of-band at issuance, the certificate lives encrypted in the subject's wallet, and per-verifier keyrings deliver exactly the minimal-disclosure presentations he describes. The guide's phrase 'trusted authority' is not a violation of his model — his framework explicitly keeps trusted issuers; what it abolishes is issuer custody and blanket disclosure, both of which the guide's design also avoids.

findings.topic: SecurityLevels Silent auto-approve vs usable-security, value-scaled friction

position_a.label: BRC llm-training-guide
position_a.claim: '0/Silent: No user interaction (auto-approve)' with recommendations 'Silent: Public tokens, read-only operations; Low: Messaging, small payments; Medium: Standard payments, certificate operations; High: Large payments, key exports, sensitive data'.
position_a.section: Section 9 'Protocol ID Design' (~lines 1315-1333) and Section 14 'Security Levels for User Experience' (~lines 1910-1924)

position_b.label: Craig Wright corpus
position_b.claim: Friction must be proportionate to stakes: usability is itself a security property, and security depth should scale with value at risk rather than being uniformly maximised.

sources.title: Security Theatre Is a Liability
sources.quote: Security that can't be used is not security.

sources.title: Security Theatre Is a Liability
sources.quote: Make the safe path the easy path.

sources.title: Digital Cash Is Not a Vault
sources.quote: One key should not control a fortune merely because one key is sufficient to buy coffee.

findings.analysis: The guide's tiered approval model — silent for inconsequential operations, explicit verification for large payments and key exports — is Craig's anti-theatre position expressed as API policy: ceremony concentrated where the value at risk justifies it, removed where it would only train users to bypass. His 'Digital Cash Is Not a Vault' argument that convenience be optimised subject to the required security level is precisely what a per-protocol security-level parameter does. The one caveat his essays would add is that Silent shifts the burden onto correct protocol-ID scoping by the application.

findings.topic: SIGHASH_NONE / ANYONECANPAY 'blank check' patterns vs the SIGHASH compositional grammar

position_a.label: BRC llm-training-guide
position_a.claim: 'Blank check: SIGHASH_NONE | ANYONECANPAY (anyone completes transaction)'; 'SIGHASH_NONE + ANYONECANPAY: anyone can complete this transaction... Enables collaborative transaction building' — taught as a deliberate flexibility pattern for token spends.
position_a.section: Section 14 'SIGHASH Flags for Transaction Flexibility' (~lines 1987-2011); Section 6 (~lines 795-805)

position_b.label: Craig Wright corpus
position_b.claim: The 2009 SIGHASH flags are the original protocol's compositional grammar of settlement, letting independent parties sign fragments that assemble into one settling transaction.

sources.title: The Immutable Stock and the Unbounded Flow
sources.quote: SIGHASH is the compositional grammar of settlement: the original source defines SIGHASH_ALL = 1, NONE = 2, SINGLE = 3, ANYONECANPAY = 0x80, letting independent parties sign fragments (their own input or output) that assemble into one settling transaction without open-ended trust.

findings.analysis: Both sides treat the SIGHASH flag matrix, including NONE and ANYONECANPAY, as legitimate original-protocol machinery for multi-party transaction assembly rather than as exotic risk. The one difference of emphasis: the guide's own label 'blank check' concedes the signature is open-ended about outputs, whereas Craig's framing stresses assembly 'without open-ended trust' — a user of the guide's pattern should note that a SIGHASH_NONE|ANYONECANPAY signature hands completion power to whoever receives it, which is fine for a 1-satoshi data token and reckless for value.

findings.topic: Automatic fee outputs at 'current fee rate' vs the priced-system, penny-fee position

position_a.label: BRC llm-training-guide
position_a.claim: 'Wallet automatically adds fee outputs'; fees are 'Based on transaction size' and use the 'current fee rate', with fee() calculating and adjusting transaction fees.

position_b.label: Craig Wright corpus
position_b.claim: Fees are prices settled between payer and miner in a priced system — admission conditioned only on validity and payment — and on a scaled chain they sit at a flat, predictable, negligible level.

sources.title: There Is No Such Thing as Spam in a Priced System
sources.quote: The alternative is arithmetic: scale the capacity, price the resource, and let payer and miner settle it between them.

sources.title: Digital Cash That Doesn't Bleed: A 11,000-Transaction Micropayment Audit Across PayPal, Stripe, Visa, Mastercard, and BSV
sources.quote: A penny beats a percent.

findings.analysis: Size-based fees paid at the going rate are exactly Craig's priced-resource model — no content classification, no admission politics, just payer and miner settling. Where his writing adds emphasis the guide does not repeat: the rate must be low and predictable (a penny-class anchor verified by CUSUM in his audit) for micropayment economics to survive, so 'current fee rate' is acceptable mechanics on BSV precisely because the fee market he criticises on BTC does not exist there. No contradiction — the guide is neutral plumbing, and the neutrality itself matches his 'price, not permission' doctrine.

findings.topic: 1-satoshi utility tokens in baskets vs token-speculation critiques

position_a.label: BRC llm-training-guide
position_a.claim: 'Tokens represent digital assets stored on-chain with minimal data footprint'; 'satoshis: minimal value (1 sat is standard for tokens)'; baskets provide 'logical grouping/categorization within wallet' — the worked examples are event tickets and hello-world data tokens, not investment instruments.

position_b.label: Craig Wright corpus
position_b.claim: Tokenisation of real-world value is Bitcoin's founding design purpose; his scorn is reserved for belief-dependent speculative tokens whose holders depend on future buyers rather than present utility.

sources.title: The Cult of Digital Metallurgy and the Poverty of Small Minds
sources.quote: The system was meant to carry value, not to imitate a bullion vault.

sources.title: The Arithmetic of the Last Fool
sources.quote: A system becomes Ponzi-like when present holders depend primarily on future buyers rather than present utility, productive yield, or transactional necessity.

sources.title: The Builder's Week: A Working Bitcoin Stack Appears, One Repository at a Time
sources.quote: Each participant posts a fixed one-satoshi bond, forfeited to the honest parties on a stale broadcast.

findings.analysis: The guide's 1-satoshi tokens are the anti-speculative extreme of tokenisation: negligible notional value, utility payloads (tickets, data, receipts), organised for accounting rather than trading. Craig's own shipped code uses one-satoshi bonds and valueless game tokens, and his metallurgy essays read tokenisation of real-world assets as Satoshi's core intent. His Ponzi-dependency test targets tokens whose only story is price appreciation; nothing in the guide's token model depends on resale, so the speculation critique passes it by.

findings.topic: SPV vs full nodes: the 'full nodes know' outlier has no Medium precedent

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: SPV is the intended and more secure user model; the non-mining 'full validation node' is a myth, and running one makes the user less secure. No Medium essay ascribes superior knowledge to full nodes over SPV clients.

sources.title: The myth of the full validation node
sources.quote: In not trusting the competitive process that is Bitcoin, in thinking her UASF node matters, she becomes less secure.

sources.title: Simplified Payment Verification
sources.quote: You cannot scale the blockchain without SPV, and more importantly, SPV is the peer aspect of Bitcoin.

sources.title: Economic Security
sources.quote: SPV is actually secure and very simple. There is no need to validate the entire blockchain, which is just the call of those with tinfoil hats.

position_b.label: Substack era (2025-2026)
position_b.claim: One Substack essay inverts the doctrine — SPV clients merely believe while full nodes know, and users are urged to run a full node — while the surrounding Substack corpus matches the Medium position exactly.

sources.title: Private Keys, Proofs, and the Illusion of Ownership in Digital Cash Systems
sources.quote: SPV clients believe; full nodes know.

sources.title: The Cult of the Full Node
sources.quote: Keeping the entire chain on a personal machine is not what makes the system secure. It is an optional hobby, a form of devotional clutter.

findings.analysis: Cross-era check on internal finding IT-01: the Medium era aggravates the collision. Nothing in 2018-2022 resembles the outlier's epistemic hierarchy; Medium Craig is uniformly militant that SPV is the white-paper model and that home validation is a security negative ('tinfoil hats'). The outlier's keys-are-access-not-title content is continuous with both eras (see XT-10); its SPV sentences contradict seven years of doctrine in both corpora. The same essay's advice to 'run a full node' is a recommendation no other essay in either corpus gives ordinary users.

findings.topic: 'Miners are nodes; home users are not nodes' — identical doctrine in both eras

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: Only miners are nodes; a non-mining 'validating node' does not exist, and UASF nodes are a fiction.

findings.analysis: Identical definition and identical rhetoric seven years apart; the Substack era adds formalisation (causal-inertness framing, the arXiv redundancy paper summarised in summary-of-the-redundancy-of-full) but no substantive change. This is the most stable technical claim across the two corpora.

findings.topic: 'Set in stone': the immutability doctrine is verbatim across eras

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: Bitcoin's protocol was fixed at v0.1; any change is a wealth transfer and a power grab, so the protocol must be locked.

sources.quote: You cannot change Bitcoin without subsidising one party and taking from another. Any change is less than a zero-sum game.

position_b.label: Substack era (2025-2026)
position_b.claim: A fixed base protocol is the precondition of value, contracting and innovation; mutability is capture.

sources.title: The Necessity of the Stone: Protocol Finality, Political Intrusion, and the Integrity of Bitcoin
sources.quote: The phrase 'set in stone' is not metaphor, nor rhetoric; it is the precise description of the foundation upon which Bitcoin was created.

findings.analysis: Slogan, rationale (long-dated contracting, removal of developer power) and framing are constant across eras. What the doctrine is asked to defend has shifted (see XT-04), but the doctrine itself never moved.

findings.topic: Rule-changes-that-restore: the Genesis paradox predates the Substack era

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: The same 2018 essays that preach 'set in stone' simultaneously promise to change the rules back — re-enabling opcodes, sunsetting P2SH — via hard fork, with the lock beginning after the restoration.

sources.title: Limited change to bring stability
sources.quote: Bitcoin cash is bitcoin and we're going to work to return it to the version 0.1.0 implementation and lock that protocol.

sources.title: Set in Stone
sources.quote: Bitcoin SV will return Bitcoin to what it was supposed to be, from the start and at 0.1. Then, we scale to the world.

sources.title: Sun-setting P2SH
sources.quote: All consensus rules in Bitcoin will be handled using the only way that works: PoW and hard forks.

position_b.label: Substack era (2025-2026)
position_b.claim: BSV's own Genesis upgrade (February 2020) — a rule change restoring opcodes — is celebrated as the enabler of the current system, while any other rule change is capture.

sources.title: The Quantum Apocalypse Is Coming Any Decade Now, So Here Is the Solution to a Problem That Will Not Exist
sources.quote: The enabler is BSV's Genesis upgrade (February 2020), which restored OP_CAT and the rest of Satoshi's opcode set.

sources.title: What Siggi Built
sources.quote: The EVM is a specification, not a venue.

findings.analysis: The internal audit's IT-12 tension is inherited, not new. The Medium era already contained both poles: absolute immutability rhetoric alongside an explicit programme of restorative rule changes (opcode re-enablement, a staged P2SH deprecation) executed by hard fork. 'Set in stone' never meant 'no further changes'; from 2018 it meant 'one more change back to 0.1, then locked'. The Substack era repeats the move with the restoration in the past tense. The paradox was never resolved, only re-dated: the lock always begins immediately after the author's preferred changes.
findings.resolution: The standing answer in both eras: restoring the original protocol is use, not revision — the stone is the 0.1 rule set, so changes returning to it are not changes. The Medium corpus shows this caveat was constitutive, not a 2026 retrofit.

findings.topic: Court-ordered freezing and reassignment: 2019 doctrine, 2026 machinery

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: Immutability is compatible with court-ordered seizure: the record never changes, but ownership can be reassigned, and miners enforce valid judicial orders.

sources.title: Proof of Assignment

sources.title: If Gold Turned to Lead

sources.title: The History of Freezing in Bitcoin
sources.quote: nodes enforce rules. A court order is a rule. Honest nodes reject blocks that don't enforce the rules.

sources.title: Good Title Is Not a Key
sources.quote: Bitcoin is recoverable.

position_b.label: Substack era (2025-2026)
position_b.claim: DAR is transparent, judicially mediated enforcement: courts decide ownership, miner compliance is mandatory, and recovery is lawful reintroduction, not theft.

sources.title: Transparency Is Not Centralisation: NAR, DAR, and the Legal Architecture of Blockchain Governance
sources.quote: The Association does not decide who owns what. Courts decide.

sources.title: The Miner Is Not a Monarch
sources.quote: does not create freedom. It creates liability.

sources.title: The Theft That Never Was
sources.quote: A recovered coin is not stolen. A dormant key is not ownership.

findings.analysis: The 2026 DAR/NAR apparatus is the operationalisation of the 2019-20 doctrine, not a departure. Two drifts worth noting: (1) Medium framed freezing as chain-agnostic — any miner on any chain would comply under jurisdiction economics ('74.1% of the BTC hash rate is located within the jurisdiction of China', good-title-is-not-a-key); Substack names BSV-specific machinery (the Association, the NAR, the Blacklist Manager). (2) The cross-era record resolves internal finding IT-02 in Craig's favour: the assignability carve-out is 2019 doctrine — immutability was always defined as immutability of the record, never of ledger state. The residual strain in both eras is rhetorical overshoot ('What's immutable can't be owned. What's fixed can't be bought.', set-in-stone-or-sold-to-the-highest) that forgets the carve-out.
findings.resolution: Resolved by the 2019 doctrine itself: immutable record, assignable ownership. DAR is the 2019 position with forms and a notary.

findings.topic: The alert key remembered two ways: enforcement prototype vs coordination signal

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: The August 2010 alert key was a prototype asset-freezing mechanism: nodes could freeze assets globally on receipt of a validly issued judicial order.

sources.title: If Gold Turned to Lead

sources.title: The History of Freezing in Bitcoin
sources.quote: Bitcoin is completely traceable, and can be frozen.

position_b.label: Substack era (2025-2026)
position_b.claim: The alert system is remembered as non-coercive coordination infrastructure whose removal merely obscured authority; the BSV Association's Alert System is its restoration.

sources.title: Authority Without Command: The Alert Key, Coordination, and the System That Might Have Been
sources.quote: It did not command, but it spoke with authority. It did not enforce, but it enabled coordination.

sources.title: Authority Without Command: The Alert Key, Coordination, and the System That Might Have Been
sources.quote: In removing it, one does not eliminate authority. One merely obscures it.

findings.analysis: The same Satoshi-era artefact is remembered as an enforcement prototype in 2019-20 (freezing on judicial orders) and as benign coordination in 2026 ('authority without command'). The enforcement memory served the freezing doctrine then; the coordination memory serves the Association's Alert System now. Both eras agree the alert key was legitimate; they differ about what it was for — and the 2026 nostalgia for foundation-style stewardship sits weeks from who-controls-the-rules-governance scoring foundation-led governance near zero (internal finding IT-07), a tension the Medium era avoided by keeping the future key-holder hypothetical.

findings.topic: Lightning as unlicensed money transmission and shadow banking

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: Lightning routing hubs are money transmitters under FinCEN/BSA; HTLCs are promissory notes; the network is a mixer that rebuilds regulated banking outside the law.

position_b.label: Substack era (2025-2026)
position_b.claim: Lightning's penalty model forces users to outsource vigilance to watchtowers and hubs, re-emerging custody and shadow banking, with legal capture following concentration.

sources.title: Lightning’s Velvet Manacles: Watchtowers, Custody, and the Quiet Return of Shadow Banking

sources.title: The Toll Road You Were Promised Would Be Free: How Refusing to Scale Rebuilds the Banks

findings.analysis: The legal theory (hubs are money transmitters; channels are promissory notes; custody re-emerges) is identical across eras. The Substack era adds the peer-reviewed topology literature as empirical vindication of the 2019 hub-concentration prediction and upgrades the rhetoric ('velvet manacles', 'shadow banking'), but the position is unchanged. The strongest cross-era continuity in the corpus.

findings.topic: Payment channels: celebrated as Satoshi's design, condemned as rent-extraction

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: nSequence/nLockTime payment channels are Satoshi's original design, disabled by BTC and to be restored; the FinCEN attack on Lightning explicitly exempts two-party Nakamoto channels that settle on-chain.

position_b.label: Substack era (2025-2026)
position_b.claim: The same channels are celebrated as original-protocol engineering — yet the toll-road essay condemns 'payment channels' undifferentiated as rent-extracting intermediaries rebuilding banks.

sources.title: The Immutable Stock and the Unbounded Flow

sources.title: The Toll Road You Were Promised Would Be Free: How Refusing to Scale Rebuilds the Banks
sources.quote: Everything else is a toll road wearing the costume of a public highway.

findings.analysis: Cross-era verdict on internal finding IT-09: the Medium era already contains the resolution. The 2018-19 corpus explicitly distinguishes bilateral Nakamoto channels (celebrated, and exempted from the money-transmitter attack because Lightning alone 'requires multiple hops and intermediaries') from routed penalty channels (condemned). The toll-road essay's categorical list is the anomaly against BOTH eras, not a new position. The Medium evidence aggravates the internal tension by showing the distinction was once load-bearing — it did legal work in the FinCEN exemption argument — and was later dropped for rhetorical sweep.
findings.resolution: The 2019 FinCEN exemption supplies the distinction the 2026 toll-road essay omits: native bilateral channels settle on-chain and complement the ledger; routed Lightning channels intermediate it.

findings.topic: 'The script is the law' vs seven years of anti-code-is-law doctrine

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: 'Code is law' is a pernicious attack on freedom; disputes belong in courts, and the assertion has long been discredited.

The anti-code-is-law doctrine is load-bearing for the whole legal edifice (DAR, keys-as-evidence, the Tulip Trading argument) and has been constant since 2018-19 — which makes the 2025 identity essay's slogan anomalous against seven years of doctrine in both eras, not a mere intra-Substack slip. The Medium evidence aggravates the collision.

findings.topic: Keys and signatures as evidence of control, never proof of ownership

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: A key is evidence of possession and no more; possession is not ownership; non-repudiation does not exist; legal effectiveness of signatures depends on statute.

findings.topic: Turing completeness of Script: same proof, more careful headline

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: Bitcoin Script is Turing complete (as a dual-stack counter machine) subject to real-world finite tape; loops are simulated by unrolling onto the alt stack; the loop omission was anti-DoS design.

sources.title: A Proof of Turing Completeness in Bitcoin Script
sources.quote: we demonstrate that Bitcoin scripting is Turing complete with the limitations imposed on any realworld computer

sources.title: Bitcoin: A Total Turing Machine
sources.quote: Bitcoin acts as a decider or Total Turing Machine

position_b.label: Substack era (2025-2026)
position_b.claim: Script is Turing-equivalent over finite bounded traces via compile-time loop unrolling (a two-pushdown automaton); the infinite-tape framing is the myth, and no consensus change is needed.

sources.title: Macro Expansion in Bitcoin Script: A Two-Stack Automaton Framework for Turing-Equivalent, Wallet-Side Contract Compilation
sources.quote: Bitcoin, when understood in this framework, is not underpowered—it is intentionally total over finite symbolic space.

sources.title: Bitcoin Script as a Macro-Expanded Turing Framework: A Compile-Time Loop Unrolling Architecture for Deterministic Contract Execution
sources.quote: It is not Bitcoin Script that fails to be Turing-complete—it is the myth of infinite computation that fails.

findings.analysis: Substance identical in both eras — the dual-stack/2PDA construction, loop unrolling ('Iterations can be simulated using an 'unrolled' loop function with allocation to the 'Alt' stack', 2018), the finite-tape caveat, and the claim that disabled opcodes (restored on BSV) complete the design. What shifted is the headline: 2018 led with 'Turing complete' and subordinated the caveat; 2025 promotes the caveat into the framing. The internal audit's noted strength (bounded formulation always stated) turns out to be a cross-era continuity — the caveat was present in 2018, just quieter.

findings.topic: One ledger vs interoperability: the constant doctrine and its two anomalies

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: One universal money on one ledger: multiple currencies are worse than barter, and sidechains or alternate chains are separate systems — not layer 2 — enabling multiple-books fraud.

sources.title: The start of Metanet
sources.quote: If every site has their own form of tradable currency, the reality is that no site has currency.

sources.title: The myth of forks
sources.quote: To put it simply, there are no forks in Bitcoin.

sources.title: Sun-setting P2SH
sources.quote: Something like a side-chain, Plasma, or the Lightning Network is a separate system; it cannot be layer 2 as it is not encapsulated in script.

position_b.label: Substack era (2025-2026)
position_b.claim: The 2025 CBDC essay rejects a single dominant system in favour of cross-chain interoperability; the 2026 essays return to one-ledger absolutism — while celebrating an EVM L2 with a bridge covenant on BSV.

sources.title: The Future of Digital Currency: The Need for Global Competition in CBDCs and Stablecoins
sources.quote: The goal should not be to create a single, dominant system controlled by one or a few entities, but rather to encourage open, competitive markets for digital currencies.

sources.title: The Graveyard of Gateways: Why There Can Only Be One Blockchain
sources.quote: If one ledger can do everything the others can do, and do it more cheaply, then fragmentation is not diversity. It is an artificial tax on users, collected by intermediaries who exist only because the market has not yet finished converging. The market will finish.

sources.title: What Siggi Built
sources.quote: The EVM is a specification, not a venue.

findings.analysis: Cross-era verdict on internal finding IT-17: the one-ledger doctrine is the constant — 2019 Medium ('no site has currency'; sidechains are 'separate systems', not layer 2) and the 2026 Graveyard essay ('fragmentation is... an artificial tax') are nearly verbatim. The 2025 CBDC essay is the anomaly against both eras, and BSVM is a second anomaly: Medium's absolute prohibition on sidechains and bridges makes a celebrated EVM L2 with a bridge covenant doubly hard to square. The charitable gloss — many currencies on one substrate; BSVM settles to BSV so it is not a separate chain — covers BSVM partially, but not the CBDC essay's explicit anti-single-dominant-system language.
findings.resolution: Partial: overlays settling to the one ledger (channels, covenant chains) are permitted by the doctrine; the CBDC essay's cross-chain ecosystem language remains unreconciled with both eras.

findings.topic: Permissionlessness: from 'collectivist lie' (2018) to the defining virtue BTC abandoned (2026)

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: 'Permission-less' is a collectivist myth: with property there cannot be permissionlessness; building is permitted within the rules, and miners must enforce law — including blocking selected addresses.

sources.title: Myths of permission-less
sources.quote: For, with property, there cannot be 'permission-less.'

sources.title: Sun-setting P2SH

sources.title: Proof of Assignment
sources.quote: Law forms a subset of rules and miners exist to enforce, not to create, such rules.

position_b.label: Substack era (2025-2026)
position_b.claim: Permissionlessness is constitutive: admission conditioned only on objective validity and payment; any sorting among paying users by purpose or 'standardness' institutes a permission regime and abandons what made the system distinctive.

sources.title: There Is No Such Thing as Spam in a Priced System
sources.quote: "permissionless" means admission conditioned only on objective validity and payment

sources.title: There Is No Such Thing as Spam in a Priced System
sources.quote: Any system that sorts among paying users by payload, purpose, "standardness" or escalating penalties has instituted a permission regime, acquired regulators, and abandoned the permissionlessness that made it distinctive.

findings.analysis: The valence inverts across eras. In 2018 permissionlessness is a myth to be debunked — property and rules come first, and by 2019-20 miners must enforce court-ordered blacklists. In 2026 permissionlessness is the constitutive virtue BTC abandoned, and any Gate-2 sorting is a permission regime — a framework under which the 2019-20 blacklist doctrine (and its 2026 heir, DAR) qualifies as exactly that. Both eras in fact contain both poles; what flipped is which pole gets the headline. A critic can now quote Craig against Craig in either direction. This is the cross-era root of internal finding IT-03.

findings.topic: Censorship resistance redefined: from validity-over-time (2019) to inclusion-access (2026)

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: Censorship resistance means a signed transaction stays valid forever and can always be replayed; the true censor is the protocol developer who changes the rules, not the state.

position_b.label: Substack era (2025-2026)

sources.title: The Two Tiers Are a Market, Not a Cage

sources.title: Censorship Resistance, Atomic Settlement, and the Limits of Coalition Power

findings.analysis: Two different idiosyncratic definitions, each serving its era's argument: 2019's validity-over-time definition serves set-in-stone; 2026's inclusion-access definition serves the two-tier market defence. The cross-era significance: under the 2019 definition, DAR is not censorship (the protocol is unchanged; a frozen output remains protocol-valid). Under the 2026 definition, a notary's blacklist preventing inclusion of a fee-paying transaction is precisely what the definition says cannot happen — internal finding IT-04. The Medium era resolves the DAR/censorship tension in Craig's favour; the 2026 redefinition manufactures it.

findings.topic: Decentralisation redefined as rule-fixity; miner oligopoly as normal market structure

On internal finding IT-05: the instrumentalist move (a controller is fine if the rules are locked) exists in both eras — on-decentralisation (2020) already argued BSV passes a regulator's control test because the protocol is locked — so the 'no governance vs named governance' tension is inherited, not new.

sources.title: The Myth of the Sovereign Node
sources.quote: Consensus in Bitcoin is not established by spectatorship.

findings.analysis: I agree with the flag. The internal evidence — first-person authorship of Hearn's Android wallet work, third-person references to Satoshi, self-citation to Hearn's blog — identifies Mike Hearn as the author; the piece is a misfiling under Craig's Medium account, most likely a repost or import artefact. It is excluded from evidence of Craig's positions in both eras. Notably, its actual content (anti-Web3, pro-SPV) is directionally consistent with Craig's doctrine anyway, so the exclusion matters for attribution hygiene rather than because the essay would distort the findings.
findings.resolution: Excluded from evidence of Craig Wright's positions; attribution to Mike Hearn accepted on internal evidence.

findings.topic: Off-chain payment channels: Satoshi's design vs fee-base subtraction

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: Two-party payment channels via nSequence/nLockTime are Satoshi's own design, a virtue of the original protocol, enabling unlimited off-chain exchange 'securely and without fees' where only the final state pays a miner fee. Channel-based micropayments are celebrated, not treated as a security threat.

sources.title: nSequence and P2P Exchange
sources.quote: the fees paid are to the miners for the settled transaction, not the exchange

sources.title: Why Lightning Will Never Be Currency, and Why BSV Matters
sources.quote: would exempt common Nakamoto payment channels and those created by Mike Hearn

position_b.label: Substack era (2025-2026)
position_b.claim: For BTC, every transaction moved off-chain is a subtraction from the fee base that must replace the subsidy; layer two is parasitic on security. Yet in the same months, bonded hash-chain channels on BSV are celebrated with the identical 'million updates, two writes' construction as the 2018 essay.

sources.title: The Defence That Halves
sources.quote: Every transaction successfully moved off-chain is a subtraction from the fee base that was supposed to replace the subsidy.

sources.title: The Immutable Stock and the Unbounded Flow
sources.quote: A channel that processes a million updates writes twice to the chain — once to open, once to close.

findings.analysis: Aggravates IE-01 from the Medium side. The 2018 essay praises exactly the property the 2026 essay condemns: off-chain exchange where miners are paid only for settlement, not for the exchange. The 2019 Lightning essay even carves two-party Nakamoto channels out of the money-transmitter analysis while condemning routed Lightning — the same mechanism-specific distinction the 2026 Defence essay abandons when it says 'every transaction successfully moved off-chain'. The 2026 BSV-channel essays (Immutable Stock, Selling the Unspent Chain) are the 2018 position restated; the 2026 BTC-channel critique contradicts it. The sorting principle is chain identity, not mechanism.
findings.resolution: Partially resolvable if the fee-subtraction argument applies only to channels that never settle at scale (BTC's routed Lightning) and not to high-volume settling channels — but the 2026 Defence essay states the subtraction principle unconditionally, and the 2018 essay explicitly frames zero-fee off-chain exchange as the design goal.

findings.topic: Layer-two security drain: chain-generic argument in 2018, BTC-only in 2026

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: The argument that an off-chain layer draining base-layer usage lowers miner revenue and therefore decreases security is stated in 2018 as a chain-generic mechanism, applied to Wormhole on BCH and Lightning on BTC alike.

sources.title: Worm-a-nomics
sources.quote: As WHC reduces use of the base layer (just as the Lightning Network does in BTC) it lowers the value of the system as a whole. This lowers the value to miners and hence, decreases the overall security of Bitcoin.

position_b.label: Substack era (2025-2026)
position_b.claim: The identical mechanism is deployed in 2026 exclusively against BTC's Lightning, while BSV's own channel constructions are exempted and celebrated in companion essays.

sources.title: The Defence That Halves
sources.quote: Layer two does not supplement the security budget; it is parasitic on it.

sources.title: Selling the Unspent Chain
sources.quote: Across the chain's whole life the ledger records two events — channel open and channel close.

findings.analysis: The Medium era proves the security-drain argument is not a 2026 invention aimed at BTC; it was part of Wright's 2018 arsenal, applied generically to any layer that moves value off the base asset. That aggravates IE-01/IE-02: he understood in 2018 that off-chain layers reduce miner revenue and security, and still celebrates channels for BSV in 2026 without auditing their effect on BSV's fee base. The 2018 version at least had a consistent scope (parasitic token layers and routed networks); the 2026 version narrows the target to BTC while widening the stated principle.

findings.topic: Security = miner revenue arithmetic: applied to BSV in 2018, BTC-only in 2026

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: The fee-revenue valuation model is applied directly and quantitatively to BSV: miners projected to earn $8,000/block from fees alone (implying $640/coin), $600,000 per terabyte block, 4M TPS by 2021, Visa running on BSV within four years.

sources.title: Valuing Systems: The Margin of Substitute Goods
sources.quote: That equates to $640 a bitcoin on exchanges, and we have not factored in the gambling price of bitcoin

sources.title: Bitcoin is a Commodity
sources.quote: With SV, we are scaling Bitcoin to handle over 4 million transactions a second in the period between now and 2021

position_b.label: Substack era (2025-2026)
position_b.claim: The security-equals-current-revenue identity is applied only to BTC's future failure; BSV's present fee base is never subjected to the same arithmetic, and the quantified 2018 predictions are never revisited.

sources.title: The Defence That Halves
sources.quote: A chain that will not scale cannot fund its own defence. The arithmetic sets the rate.

sources.title: The Asset That Pays Rent to Exist
sources.quote: BTC is a flow — a service that must be re-purchased from the physical world continuously

findings.analysis: Aggravates IE-02 decisively. The 2026 asymmetry (audit BTC's security budget, never BSV's) cannot be defended as a consistent methodological choice, because the 2018 essays show Wright once did apply the arithmetic to his own chain — and every quantified prediction failed (BSV never reached millions of TPS, Visa never came, the $640 floor never held). The retreat from self-application followed the failure of the predictions, which is the pattern a critic would cite first.

findings.topic: Fixed supply vs state power: defanging bureaucrats vs 'men cannot be governed by code'

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: Bitcoin's fixed supply strips the state and its bureaucrats of monetary power; betting on Bitcoin is betting on something that cannot be devalued at a whim. Bitcoin is 'sound money, a stable supply'.

sources.title: Keynesian Flaws
sources.quote: In controlling the money supply, they have power over all our lives. With Bitcoin, these un-elected bureaucrats lose much of this ill gained power.

sources.title: A Diatribe on Bitcoin, Trust and the Economy of Security (Redux)
sources.quote: You may bet on currency controlled by state player and I will bet on something that is decentralised and which cannot be devalued at a whim.

sources.title: Bitcoin is for Business
sources.quote: Bitcoin was never about removing banks and government. It is sound money, a stable supply, and an efficient and audit-able ledger

position_b.label: Substack era (2025-2026)
position_b.claim: No monetary mechanism constrains the state; states borrow, suspend and debase under any reserve asset, and a Bitcoin Standard would fail for the same reason gold failed.

sources.title: The Myth of the Bitcoin Standard
sources.quote: Gold failed because it assumed men could be governed by metal. Bitcoin will fail because it assumes men can be governed by code.

findings.analysis: Aggravates IE-07 from the Medium side. The 2018 essays make the disciplinary claim in its strong form: Bitcoin removes the power to devalue, and this is the answer to Keynesian central planning. The 2025 essay makes the anti-disciplinary claim in its strong form: scarcity cannot substitute for discipline, and every inflation is a partial default that continues regardless of the reserve asset. Both are load-bearing for their eras' worldviews — 2018 Craig is a recognisable sound-money anti-inflationist; 2025 Craig treats that position as a category error about men and institutions.
findings.resolution: A narrow reconciliation exists (Bitcoin removes the power to print the base asset, not the power to issue claims on it), but the 2018 rhetoric ('cannot be devalued at a whim', bureaucrats 'lose power') promises more than that narrow point, and the 2025 essay denies even its spirit.

findings.topic: Miner deviation: selfish-mining-as-FUD vs measured deviation-dominance

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: Selfish-mining and deviation analyses are dismissed as pseudoscientific FUD; mining is memoryless, rational miners always work on the next block, and profitable deviation does not exist.

sources.title: Miners and Rational Expectations
sources.quote: the miner expects the next block at 10 mins from now — ALWAYS

sources.title: The Great Mining Swindle
sources.quote: There is no threat of mystic pseudoscientific FUD spreading such as 'selfish mining'

position_b.label: Substack era (2025-2026)
position_b.claim: Deviation from cooperative validation is the rational equilibrium in fee-dominant regimes across almost all simulated runs, even at low fee volatility.

sources.title: The Nash Equilibrium in Digital Cash
sources.quote: Fee-dominant regimes (κ = 0.10–0.30) are deviation-dominant in 93.75% of runs even at low fee volatility

findings.analysis: Aggravates IE-03. The 2018-19 essays deny the phenomenon absolutely and attack the academics who model it; the 2026 essay measures precisely when deviation pays and finds it dominant exactly in the fee-dominant end-state the 2018-19 essays prescribe as Bitcoin's destiny. The reconciliation (subsidy-anchored revenue and stable rules keep cooperation; fee-dominance plus volatility breaks it) is available in the 2026 model but is nowhere acknowledged as a concession to the literature he mocked.
findings.resolution: Implicitly resolved by the 2026 model's cooperative equilibria under subsidy-dominant, low-volatility regimes — the conditions the 2018 essays assumed — but the rhetorical absolutism of 2018-19 stands unretracted.

findings.topic: Hoarding: an incoherent slur vs a moral vice

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: 'Hoarding' as an economic category is denied outright; saving and large holdings are legitimate differences in risk appetite, no different from holding land. HODL is condemned separately as uninformed speculation, and 'spend and replace' is urged.

sources.title: Hoarding and Bitcoin
sources.quote: There is no such thing as hoarding. That is our differences in the risk appetite of individuals.

position_b.label: Substack era (2025-2026)
position_b.claim: Hoarding is the central vice of the BTC cult: to hoard is to rot, and you cannot hoard your way to money.

sources.title: You Cannot Hoard Your Way to Money
sources.quote: You cannot brand your way to money, you cannot litigate your way to money, and above all you cannot hoard your way to money.

sources.title: Where Your Treasure Is
sources.quote: To hold, in the true Biblical sense, is to steward. To hoard is to rot.

findings.analysis: Predates and sharpens IE-19. Both eras condemn idle never-spend holding, so the underlying economics is continuous. What changed is the treatment of the category itself: 2018 Wright defends the holder against the hoarding slur ('we do not run around calling land holders hoarders'), while 2025-26 Wright makes hoarding a moral failing at the centre of his critique of BTC. A critic can put 'There is no such thing as hoarding' (2018) next to 'You cannot hoard your way to money' (2026) as a slogan-level collision; the substance (use gives value, saving is fine) survived intact.
findings.resolution: The 2018 essay already contains the Substack position in embryo (HODL as 'uninformed speculation'); the shift is one of moral register, not doctrine.

findings.topic: Banks and intermediaries: pro-bank Medium vs the $40T skim

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: Bitcoin does not replace banks, central banks, or credit; fractional-reserve banking is defended against critics who 'don't understand how it actually works'; payment intermediaries are praised as enforcement gatekeepers, and only the inefficient card-network rails are marked for replacement.

sources.title: Bitcoin is Not Against Banks
sources.quote: Bitcoin doesn't stop banking, it doesn't even stop central banks.

sources.title: The Way You Explain How Bitcoin Can Not Stop Debt...
sources.quote: The way you explain how Bitcoin can not stop debt, convinces me that you don't understand how fractional-reserve banking actually works.

sources.title: Payment Intermediaries
sources.quote: As the financial gatekeepers, payment intermediaries can be used to prevent illicit activity over the Internet

position_b.label: Substack era (2025-2026)
position_b.claim: Financial intermediation as a sector is a parasitic caste consuming some $40T of global output while producing nothing; the anti-bank movement merely rebuilt banking in hoodies.

sources.title: The Great Global Skim
sources.quote: more than US$40 trillion each year to a caste that produces nothing but movement without progress

sources.title: The Priesthood of Artificial Scarcity
sources.quote: The anti-bank movement rebuilt banking. Only this time the banks are wrapped in hoodies and Twitter memes.

findings.analysis: Aggravates IE-17. The Medium era is uniformly in the 'defended functions' camp for banks and credit — the polemical target is only the card networks ('ineffective payment systems (such as Visa and MasterCard)'). The maximalist anti-intermediation register is a Substack novelty. The careful Substack essays (the Toll Booth value test, the surviving functions in When Money Moves for Free) restore the Medium position, so the collision is between Medium's doctrine and Substack's satire, with Substack's analysis siding with Medium.
findings.resolution: The Toll Booth Economy (2026-05-17) supplies the reconciliation: 'Intermediaries are justified only when they reduce the costs of exchange more than they increase dependency, delay, rent extraction and control' — a test the Medium pro-bank essays implicitly apply and pass.

findings.topic: One money vs many currencies

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: A multiplicity of coins and tokens is worse than barter; one universal money is required, and a world where every site has its own currency is a world where no site has currency.

sources.title: The Start of Metanet
sources.quote: If every site has their own form of tradable currency, the reality is that no site has currency… it is a system that is less effective than barter.

position_b.label: Substack era (2025-2026)
position_b.claim: The future is multiple CBDCs and stablecoins cooperating across chains, with no single dominant system as the explicit goal.

sources.title: The Future of Digital Currency
sources.quote: The goal should not be to create a single, dominant system controlled by one or a few entities

findings.analysis: Extends IE-15 backward: the one-money doctrine is 2019 Metanet, not a late hardening. The reconciliation (many currencies as tokens on one ledger, so the unit-of-account multiplicity sits atop a single money) is available from the tokenisation essays in both eras, but neither the 2019 polemic nor the 2025 policy essay states it cleanly.
findings.resolution: Implicitly resolved by the one-ledger-many-tokens architecture (tokenised fiat on a single chain), present in Medium's Tokenized essays and Substack's stablecoin essays alike.

findings.topic: Fee levels: 2018 targets vs 2025 measured anchor

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: Fees are specified in a tight, USD-denominated band and promised to fall: $0.004-0.008/KB tiers, ~$0.005 per standard transaction, under $0.001 for a simple record transaction, ~$0.0025 average at scale.

sources.title: Subsidised Ledgers
sources.quote: Over time, and as the system grows in use and value, we would expect this to become even cheaper for users

sources.title: Taking Care of Business
sources.quote: under $0.001 USD for a simple record transaction

position_b.label: Substack era (2025-2026)
position_b.claim: The celebrated measured anchor on BSV is roughly $0.01 per transaction, while modelled figures range from $0.0001 down to a $0.00000002 cost floor.

sources.title: Digital Cash That Doesn't Bleed
sources.quote: BSV's flat, penny-class fee (anchored at roughly $0.01)

sources.title: When Money Moves for Free
sources.quote: ~$0.00000002 per transaction

findings.analysis: Extends IE-05 across eras. The direction of travel (sub-cent, falling) is continuous, but the 2025 measured 'penny anchor' is roughly ten times the 2018 merchant promise of under $0.001 — the ecosystem's actual fees drifted above his own published targets, unremarked, while the modelled figures drifted orders of magnitude below them. The Medium band is internally tight; the Substack scatter is six orders of magnitude wide. Neither era reconciles its own numbers.

findings.topic: The Ponzi label: thrown freely vs expressly retracted

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: BTC is called a Ponzi outright, and Bitcoin generally is framed as either commodity money or a Ponzi.

sources.title: The Labour Fallacy of Bitcoin Value
sources.quote: In the case of Bitcoin Core (BTC), we have a speculative gambling asset, a Ponzi that is designed to pump until, well, it doesn't.

sources.title: Bitcoin is a Commodity
sources.quote: The result is that Bitcoin is either commodity money or a pure Ponzi.

position_b.label: Substack era (2025-2026)
position_b.claim: The Ponzi label is explicitly analysed and withdrawn as technically inapplicable.

sources.title: The Defence That Halves
sources.quote: Of the three Ponzi elements, one holds and two do not, so the term should not be used.

findings.analysis: A genuine rhetorical maturation: the 2026 essay does the element-by-element analysis the 2018 essays skipped, and reaches the disciplined conclusion against his own earlier usage. The substantive critique (earlier participants paid from later ones) is retained; only the label is surrendered.
findings.resolution: Resolved by the 2026 element analysis — the label was always doing work the argument did not need.

findings.topic: The 21 million figure: slogan vs integer-truncation artefact

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: The 2019 halving essay already treats 21 million as an approximation produced by the geometric series and integer limits, with the subsidy disappearing around 2140; the 2020 explainer uses the slogan form.

sources.title: Zeno's Paradoxes and Bitcoin
sources.quote: at least as an approximate figure

sources.title: Bitcoin System Has 21 Million Bitcoin Tokens
sources.quote: 1 BitCoin is shorthand for 100 million satoshis

position_b.label: Substack era (2025-2026)
position_b.claim: October 2025 repeats the slogan ('twenty-one million coins with halving intervals written into code'); May 2026 corrects it ('There are no decimals in Bitcoin. There is no twenty-one million.'), giving the exact summation.

sources.title: The Necessity of the Stone
sources.quote: twenty-one million coins with halving intervals written into code

sources.title: The Integer and the Idol
sources.quote: There are no decimals in Bitcoin. There is no twenty-one million.

findings.analysis: Predates IE-08: the Medium era already contains both registers — the 2019 Zeno essay is the technical correction in embryo, the 2020 explainer the slogan. The Substack oscillation between slogan and correction is therefore not new; what is new is the 2026 essay's polemical framing of the correction against the 'idol' of the number itself.
findings.resolution: The 2019 Zeno essay and the 2026 Integer essay agree; the slogan usages in both eras are the outliers.

findings.topic: Finality: actuarial 'safe enough' vs 'transactions, once made, are final'

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: Settlement is explicitly probabilistic and actuarial: 0-conf is safe enough for vending machines, blocks are sufficiently irreversible in an hour or so, and there is no such thing as 100% safe.

sources.title: Economic Security
sources.quote: There is no such thing as 100% safe. There is only safe enough.

sources.title: Bitcoin (BCH) Vending Machine
sources.quote: secure enough for most purposes

position_b.label: Substack era (2025-2026)
position_b.claim: The payments essays assert flat finality, while the security essays reassert probabilistic settlement.

sources.title: When the Tollkeepers Disappear
sources.quote: Transactions, once made, are final.

sources.title: The Dial That Used to Be Fixed
sources.quote: Settlement is probabilistic, subject to fork and reorganisation

findings.analysis: Resolves IE-11 in favour of the probabilists, from the Medium side: the absolute-finality register is a Substack payments-essay novelty that the 2018-19 actuarial doctrine contradicts. The Medium era never promised protocol finality; it priced residual fraud risk against cash-handling losses, which is exactly the 2026 Dial essay's position.
findings.resolution: The Medium actuarial doctrine and the Substack security essays agree; the Substack payments slogans are the outlier in both eras' company.

findings.topic: Gold: trust anchor vs failed discipline

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: Gold's non-printability is the genuine anchor of monetary trust ('you cannot print gold'), and its value lies precisely in the limitations it imposes on issuers.

sources.title: A Diatribe on Bitcoin, Trust and the Economy of Security (Redux)
sources.quote: you cannot print gold

sources.title: Money is Time and Energy
sources.quote: The value of gold lies in the limitations it imposes.

position_b.label: Substack era (2025-2026)
position_b.claim: Gold's monetary discipline failed historically and was always going to; gold's monetary role was historical, not metaphysical.

sources.title: The Myth of the Bitcoin Standard
sources.quote: Gold failed because it assumed men could be governed by metal.

findings.analysis: A three-waypoint evolution: 2018 gold-philic Mengerianism, 2020 nuance (no intrinsic value, discipline only, black-swan discoveries acknowledged), 2025 anti-disciplinarianism. The movement is consistent in direction — away from commodity-money romanticism toward institutional pessimism — but the 2018 essay deploys exactly the 'cannot print' argument the 2025 essay treats as the original delusion. Aggravates IE-07 alongside XE-04.
findings.resolution: The 2020 essay is the hinge: gold's limits have value but no metaphysical guarantee. The 2025 essay completes the retreat.

findings.topic: Price theory: Hayekian discovery vs barometer of arousal

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: Prices are the epistemic machinery of the economy; the pricing system is why central planning fails.

sources.title: Hidden Costs
sources.quote: this is why there is no agreement and why we need the pricing system

position_b.label: Substack era (2025-2026)
position_b.claim: Price is not a measure of worth but a barometer of collective arousal and tension.

sources.title: Ventriloquising the Void
sources.quote: Price, then, is not a measure of worth but of collective arousal. It is a barometer of tension, not truth.

findings.analysis: Aggravates IE-09 from the Medium side: the 2018 essay is orthodox Hayek, and the 2025 barometer essay contradicts both eras' Austrian price epistemology. The barometer register remains the outlier against a two-era consensus.
findings.resolution: The barometer essay is best read as a critique of speculative asset prices specifically, though its sentence is stated without that restriction.

findings.topic: Miners: income-earning contractors vs ideological loss-makers

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: Two registers coexist in November 2018: miners are paid 'an income for the completion of a task' with empty-block miners as parasites, and — thirteen days earlier, mid hash-war — mining at a loss for years is celebrated as long-term ideological strategy.

sources.title: Subsidised Ledgers
sources.quote: an income for the completion of a task

sources.title: Sustaining Hash
sources.quote: not profitable to maintain... yet, we will for the long-term gains

position_b.label: Substack era (2025-2026)
position_b.claim: The security model assumes economically rational miners whose aggregate expenditure equals revenue; zero-profit binds at the margin.

sources.title: The Defence That Halves
sources.quote: Proof-of-work converts current expense into defence, equal to current miner revenue.

findings.analysis: The 2018 hash-war doctrine (sustained loss-mining for ideological ends) sits awkwardly with both the same-month income framing and the 2026 model: if miners can rationally mine at a loss for years, then security expenditure can exceed revenue and the security-equals-revenue identity breaks in the other direction. The 2026 model quietly assumes away the actor the 2018 essay celebrated.
findings.resolution: The 2026 model notes expenditure is at or below revenue under heterogeneous costs; the 2018 loss-mining episode shows it can also exceed revenue — neither essay acknowledges the other's regime.

findings.topic: Subsidy as bootstrap, fees as destiny

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: The block subsidy is a temporary contractual bootstrap payment, explicitly not a reward, and fee revenue from transaction volume must replace it for the system to continue existing — stated with Satoshi's own fee-transition remark and a concrete deadline.

sources.title: Commodity and Security
sources.quote: the fees at this point will be critical to the continued existence of the system

sources.title: Bitcoin is All About Incentives
sources.quote: In a few decades when the reward gets too small, the transaction fee will become the main compensation for nodes

sources.title: Schnorr
sources.quote: BTC must be funded by competitive on-chain fees — a marginal cost of around 0.005 USD a transaction — no more... or the miners will leave the chain.

position_b.label: Substack era (2025-2026)
position_b.claim: Identical doctrine, identical vocabulary.

sources.title: The Defence That Halves
sources.quote: The subsidy was scaffolding. The fee market was the building.

sources.title: Bitcoin After the Casino
sources.quote: high volume multiplied by low fees

findings.analysis: The load-bearing continuity of the entire corpus: the security-budget doctrine is stated in 2018 with the same structure, the same Satoshi citation, and even the same scaffolding metaphor as 2026. This is the fixed point against which XE-01, XE-02 and XE-03 measure the selective application. Its cross-era stability is also what makes the non-application to BSV (IE-02) a choice rather than an oversight.
findings.resolution: Not a collision — the single most stable doctrine in the corpus.

findings.topic: No such thing as spam: use is the point

position_a.label: Medium era (2018-2022)
position_a.claim: Calling paid, rule-valid transactions 'spam' is a pernicious lie; the system is designed to incentivise use, and any paid transaction is legitimate.

sources.title: Subsidised Ledgers
sources.quote: designed to incentivise use, the same thing some call spam

sources.title: Bitcoin is a Commodity
sources.quote: There is no spam on the blockchain that is paid for.

position_b.label: Substack era (2025-2026)
position_b.claim: Identical doctrine, elevated to a title.

sources.title: There Is No Such Thing as Spam in a Priced System
sources.quote: a fee-paying, rule-valid transaction

findings.analysis: Verbatim continuity across eight years: the 2026 essay's admission-control-equals-governance argument is the 2018 position with a game-theoretic veneer. Included as a finding because the anti-spam doctrine is load-bearing for the fee-volume security model of XE-16 — volume must never be filtered, because volume is the security budget.
findings.resolution: Not a collision.

strengths_observed.note: The privacy/anonymity/secrecy taxonomy is applied uniformly — privacy via lawful scale plus auditable off-chain records, anonymity rejected for payments, and the one exception (true anonymity for votes) is explicitly argued as a category distinction, not smuggled in.
'A private key is control, not title' is held consistently across custody, property and law essays spanning ten months.

Script expressiveness is always claimed as bounded/finite-trace Turing equivalence with the limitation stated aloud — the corpus never inflates it into 'world computer' rhetoric, and treats Ethereum's unbounded model as the cautionary counter-case.
Tokenisation and data-on-chain are consistently framed as the design purpose (timestamping, proof, property records) while token speculation is consistently the pathology — the line does not move.

The two-regime security model (protocol-only deterrence for small payments, protocol-plus-law for large ones) recurs unchanged across the security-economics cluster, with Budish contained rather than hand-waved.

The security-budget dichotomy (subsidy scaffolding → fee replacement; 'massive volume at low fees or tiny volume at high fees', with the flow identity security = current miner revenue) is stated identically and mutually consistently across at least five essays spanning a year.
The anti-hoarding / unit-of-account-follows-the-medium-of-exchange position (White 1984) is applied with the same logic and same conclusion across theological, satirical and formal registers.

The fractional-reserve arithmetic is internally coherent: 'perhaps five per cent' real coins, 'one coin, three claims', and 'twenty-to-one... a benchmark of efficiency' are the same ratio restated, and the 1971-suspension endgame is argued identically in each.

Producer/validator count is treated with one consistent interior-optimum logic everywhere: five-to-twenty industrial miners is healthy, too many validators subtract security, and underfunded miner populations fail — no essay argues 'more is better' or 'fewer is fatal' in isolation.

Price-scepticism is epistemically disciplined and symmetric: fitted curves are 'numerology with regression output', retrodiction has no predictive authority, Finney's wealth-divided-by-supply formula is numerology, and the corpus never uses BTC or BSV price appreciation as evidence for its own claims — even the Ponzi label is expressly qualified ('one holds... so the term should not be used').

'Private, not anonymous' is a verbatim formula in both eras: privacy requires traceability, and anonymity is framed as the enemy of honest money ('It is not anonymous, it is private', 2018; pseudonymity as 'accountability without exposure', 2025).
'Bitcoin uses no encryption — all transactions are conducted in clear text' is asserted identically in both eras.

A small miner oligopoly is the designed equilibrium in both eras; only the headcount drifts ('five or more' mining entities in 2018; '100 miners globally' in 2020; 'five to twenty serious miners' in 2025).
The same word-count exegesis — 'honest' appears 15 times in the white paper, keyed to the UK Fraud Act 2006 — is repeated verbatim seven years apart.

'A changed protocol is not Bitcoin': a fork with different rules is an airdrop copy, and keeping the ticker is a hijack ('If you copy it and release a fork with different protocol rules, it is not Bitcoin', 2019; 'BTC is no longer Bitcoin. It is a ticker hijack with marketing muscle', 2025).

The Satoshi origin story is always within-law — but the founding grievance drifts: 2019 essays ground the design in stopping Liberty Reserve-style criminal money, while the 2025 essay grounds it in the 2007-08 payment strangulation of online gambling.

Zero-confirmation acceptance as ordinary commercial risk management ('You don't fix double spends, you detect them', 2019; the merchant 'need only obtain enough information to make a rational decision', 2026) is identical across eras.

Anti-digital-gold and anti-store-of-value: 'store of value' is a property of contracts, not assets; holding bitcoin does not make it one; 'digital gold' is a category error serving only money-laundering. Stated in 2019 and restated with cult vocabulary in 2025-26.

Money as measuring stick / ledger of obligations, stability over appreciation: money is a measurement of stored debt; a money that rises is a failed measuring stick; Bitcoin should be stable and boring. The 2025-26 'number that must never rise' and 'scoreboard is not the game' essays restate the 2019-20 doctrine almost verbatim.

Security is economic, not cryptographic: Bitcoin's protection is expenditure and incentive, not mathematics; residual risk is priced actuarially ('safe enough', never 100%). The 2019 essay and the 2026 security cluster are the same doctrine.

Lightning as re-intermediation and regulatory exposure: routed Lightning nodes are money transmitters under BSA/FinCEN, a shadow-banking reconstruction that destroys records. The 2019 FINRA/MSB essays and the 2025-26 'velvet manacles'/'rebuilt banking' essays are continuous in both economics and law.

Tokenised fiat on-chain as design fulfilment, Tether as fraud: bank-issued fiat tokens settling on Bitcoin plumbing realise Satoshi's 'backed with cash' remark, while Tether specifically is condemned as a Ponzi of unbacked digital rights. Concept endorsed, instantiation condemned, in both eras.

Micropayments as the moral and economic mission: sub-cent fees unlock microwork for the world's poor and machine-to-machine commerce; this is why scaling matters. The 2018 African-microwork essay and the 2025 nano-economy essays share argument and register.

Energy buys security, not value: the labour/energy theory of value is a Marxian fallacy; value comes from subjective demand and use. The 2018 labour-fallacy essays and the 2025-26 scarcity critiques ('the energy is not buying throughput; it is buying scarcity') apply the same subjective-value doctrine.

Commodity ledger theory: Bitcoin's commodity is ledger space — the right to an immutable entry — purchased via the token; demand comes from businesses paying to record data and contracts. The 2018 commodity essays and the 2025-26 tokenisation/Metanet essays share this foundation.
